events.event_narrative: High water was observed in several areas around the county, including Charleston Road in the town of Red House and Winfield Road. A few road closures also occurred due to flooding, including Harbor Lane and Hurricane Creek Road over in Hurricane.
Near the town of Speed, high water was observed along the roadway at the intersection of US-119 and Speed Road.
Several road closures occurred due to flooding around the county, including Coopers Creek Road as well as New Goff Mountain Road in Cross Lanes.

Several of the major roadways in Athens County were closed from the morning of the 18th until the next day due to high water along the roadways. These included SR-13, SR-329, SR-356, SR-56, SR-681, and Oakdale Road.

High water was observed along several roadways on the evening of the 17th, including the intersection of White Oak Road and Ohio State Route 554, the intersection of Hannan Trace Road and Ohio State Route 775, and along Ohio State Route 850.
All lanes of State Route 775 North were closed due to high water as were several other major roadways in the county. This included State Route 233 West and State Route 554 East.
All lanes of State Route 139 were closed due to high water from Spruce Hollow Road down to State Route 279.
All lanes of State Route 124 were closed due to high water from State Route 325 to State Route 7.

All lanes of State Route 376 were closed early on the morning of the 18th due to high water from Taylor Drive to State Route 266. Later that morning, State Route 78 East also closed due to flooding from Township Road to State Route 83.

Along State Route 668 from State Route 204 to Township Road 65, all lanes were closed due to flooding. All lanes of State Route 204 were also closed due to high water near the intersection of Gower Road. State Route 93 also observed water from State Route 13 to Township Road 402, resulting in road closures.
All of the westbound lanes of State Route 56 beyond Locust Grove Road were shut down due to high water.

State Route 821 observed high water from Cumberland Road to Broad Street, resulting in all lanes to be closed. All lanes of State Route 145 South were closed from Schott Hollow Road to Thompson Street due to flooding.
High water was observed on the southbound side of Roxalana Road at Lower Midway Drive in Dunbar.

High water and debris flowed along Route 119 between Walton and Gandeeville which resulted in road closures in several spots. Spring Creek rose out of its banks and spilled onto Front Street in the town of Spencer. Johnson Creek Road observed high water as the nearby creek rose out of its banks.

In the town of Whipple, Duck Creek rose out of its 12 foot bankfull level late on the evening of February 3rd. The creek crested at 15.39 feet the next afternoon then returned to its banks during the predawn hours of February 5th. Minor flooding occurred along State Routes 26, 821, and 145 while Duck Creek was out of its banks.

Duck Creek near the town of Whipple rose out of its 12 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 18th. After midnight the creek crested at 14.33 feet then returned to its banks after sunrise on the 19th. With the creek out of its banks, minor flooding occurred along State Routes 26, 821, and 145.

The Hocking River at Athens rose out of its 20 foot flood stage late in the afternoon on February 19th. The river remained above its flood stage for only a brief period of time and was back in its banks that evening. Low lying areas around the river and the nearby campground observed minor flooding between Athens and Coolville while the Hocking River was out of its banks.

The Little Muskingum River near Bloomfield rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level just before sunrise on the 18th. The river crested at 20.64 feet that afternoon before returning to its banks just after midnight. This resulted in minor flooding at the intersection of Route 26 and Route 260 along with minor flooding at the nearby hay field adjacent to the river.

In Bloomfield, the Little Muskingum River rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level on the afternoon of February 25th. The river crested at 18.84 feet that evening then returned to its banks very early on the 26th. While out of its banks, the river spilled onto State Route 260 where it intersects with Route 26.

In the town of Little, Middle Island Creek rose out of its 14 foot bankfull level on the afternoon of February 18th. After cresting at 14.78 a few hours later the creek returned to its banks. Minor flooding along the fields adjacent to the creek occurred while it was out of its banks.

Middle Island Creek near the town of Middlebourne rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 18th and remained out of its banks until that afternoon. The creek crested at 17.31 feet, which resulted in minor flooding of a nearby field and low drainage areas adjacent to the creek.

The Muskingum River at Beverly rose out of its 29 foot flood stage just after midnight on the 18th and would not return to its banks until the afternoon of the 19th. While in flood stage, the river crested at 33.28 feet and resulted in flooding of nearby fields, farmlands, and homes. High water crept close to Route 60, but only reached the local roads in Beverly that reside south of Route 60.

The Muskingum River in Beverly rose out of its 29 foot flood stage during the early evening hours of February 25th. The river crested at 29.8 feet a few hours later and returned to its banks just after midnight on the 26th. Fields and farmlands residing adjacent to the river observed minor flooding while the Muskingum River was out of its banks.

In the town of Beverly, the Muskingum River rose out of its 29 foot flood stage late in the evening of February 22nd, cresting at 30.72 feet during the predawn hours of the 26th, and returning to its banks later that evening. Floodwaters spilled onto the nearby fields and farmlands while the river was out of its banks.

The Muskingum River in McConnelsville rose out of its 11 foot flood stage on the evening of February 22nd. Just after midnight on the 23rd, the river crested at 11.59 feet and returned to its banks just before noon that morning. Several roads observed high water spilling from the river, including Route 669 near Malta and down into McConnelsville. Several homes near the river also observed minor flooding.

During the early morning hours of February 18th, the Muskingum River in McConnelsville rose out of its 11 foot flood stage. The river crested at 12.66 feet late that morning and did not return to its banks until the afternoon of February 19th. While out of its banks, much of the town of McConnelsville was flooded as well as State Route 376 and State Route 669. Many homes in the town observed flooding in their yards.

The Belleville Lock of the Ohio River observed the river rising out of its 35 foot flood stage on the morning of February 19th. The river crested at 36.53 feet just before sunrise on the 20th and returned to its banks that evening. While this portion of the Ohio River was in flood, Ohio State Route 124, which resides adjacent to the river up to the Meigs/Washington County line, flooded as well as smaller roads that feed into Route 124.

The Ohio River at Point Pleasant rose above its 40 foot flood stage on the evening of February 26th. The river crested at 40.86 feet around noon on the 17th and returned to its banks early in the morning on February 28th. Low lying areas surrounding Point Pleasant became inundated from the backwaters of the river. The lower pier of the amphitheater in the town was underwater and several roads observed high water, including Salt Creek Road, Hannan Trace Road, Huntington Road at Boggs Run Road, and Mason Eighty Road.

The Shade River rose above its 17 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 18th, cresting at 17.88 feet a few hours later, then returned to its banks just after midnight on the 19th. Minor flooding of low lying areas occurred along the river and high water was observed on the Sugar Run Creek Bridge and the Shade River Bridge.

In the town of Mill Creek, the Tygart Valley River rose above its 11 foot bankfull level just before sunrise on the 4th, cresting at 12.24 around noon, then returned to its banks late that evening. Backwater from the river spilled onto portions of Route 39 while out of its banks.

The West Fork of Duck Creek in Macksburg rose out of its 13 foot bankfull level early on February 18th. After cresting at 15.57 feet late that evening, the creek returned to its banks after daybreak on the 19th. This resulted in flooding across fields and campgrounds adjacent to the creek as well as several homes. High water also spilled onto State Route 81 and Broad Street.

In Macksburg, Duck Creek rose above its 13 foot bankfull level just after midnight on February 23rd. The creek crested at 13.44 feet around noon that day and returned to its banks a few hours later. While the creek was out of its banks, minor flooding occurred in fields and campgrounds within close vicinity of the gage.

In the early afternoon hours of February 25th, the West Fork of Duck Creek rose out of its 13 foot bankfull level, cresting at 13.55 feet just after midnight on the 26th, and returned to its banks a few hours later. Backwater from the creek resulted in minor flooding of nearby fields and campgrounds.

A tornado continued from Hocking County into Vinton County. The tornado uprooted and snapped numerous hardwood trees across northern Vinton County from Macedonia Road eastward to Goosecreek Road. The tornado lifted between Goosecreek Road and Locust Grove Road.

A swath of trees with signs of convergence/rotation occurred on the northwest side of the ridge between Lake Hope and the Lake Hope State Park Lodge and Cabins. Multiple large healthy trees, including Oak and Hickory, were snapped and uprooted. A tree on the outer edge of the damage path fell onto a cabin causing minor damage.

A group of trees were uprooted with some smaller trees snapped near a campsite and backpacking trail in the Zaleski State Forest. The trees showed signs of convergence. Due to dense forest and limitation of ground survey, it is unknown how far the damage path actually went into the forest. However, additional tree damage found in a logged area farther east on King Hollow Road was likely the eastward extent of the path.

In the town of Buckhannon, the gage along the Buckhannon River observed a rise above its 23 foot bankfull level on the afternoon of May 7th. The river crested at midnight at 24.7 feet before returning to its banks the next morning. Portions of Cleveland Avenue and Wood Street were under water while the river was out of its banks as well as sections of Route 20.

The Little Kanawha River in Glenville above its 23 foot flood stage on the morning of May 7th and did not return to its banks until after midnight on the 8th. The river crested at 26.48 feet, which resulted in minor flooding within the township, including portions of Elm Street and South Street. A few homes adjacent to the river also observed ponding in their front yards.

The Middle Fork of the Mud River rose out of its 12 foot bankfull level near Griffithsville on the evening of May 6th. The river only remained out of its banks for a few hours and crested at 12.24 feet. While out of its banks, the fields located adjacent to the river were inundated with water.

In the town of Little, Middle Island Creek rose out of its 14 foot bankfull level and remained out of its banks until the early morning hours of May 8th. The creek rose to 14.47 feet, which resulted in minor flooding along Stewarts Run Road and within the field located opposite of the gage.

Middle Island Creek in Middlebourne rose out of its 16 bankfull level in the early afternoon hours of May 7th. The creek rose to 17.38 feet before returning to its banks just after midnight on the 8th. Minor flooding of nearby fields occurred while the creek was out of its banks.

On the morning of May 7th, Middle Island Creek near the town of West Union rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level. The creek rose to 18.10 feet before returning to its banks later that evening. During which time, minor flooding was observed along Route 18 and into the Doddridge County Park.

The Ohio River at Point Pleasant rose above its 40 foot flood stage on the evening of May 8th. The river would remain out of its banks until the early morning hours of May 10th and crested at 41.7 feet. This resulted in minor flooding around low lying spots of Point Pleasant, including the town's amphitheater.

The Tygart River near Ellamore rose above its 13 foot bankfull level during the late morning hours of May 7th. The river crested at 14.05 feet, which resulted in water spilling onto County Road 28, before returning to its banks later that evening.

The gage along the Tygart Valley River in Belington observed the river rising above its bankfull level of 14 feet on the afternoon of May 7th. The river continued to oscillate in and out of its banks until the next morning, and crested at 14.46 feet. Before fully returning to its banks, water spilled onto roads located in close vicinity to the river, including River and Dayton Streets, the intersections of Talbott Road, and Walbash Street.

The Tygart River near the town of Mill Creek rose above its 11 foot bankfull level on the morning of May 7th, crested at 12.14 feet, then returned to its banks late that night. Water spilled onto County Road 39 while the river was out of its banks.

On the afternoon of May 7th, the Tygart River in Philippi rose above its 19 foot flood stage and resulted in flooding along portions of Route 119 and Route 250 as well as smaller streets including Sycamore Street and Beech Avenue. The river returned to its banks a few hours after midnight on the 8th.

The West Fork River in Clarksburg rose above its 14 foot flood stage on the evening of May 7th and remained in flood until the early morning hours of the 8th. The river crested at 14.31 feet, which resulted in minor flooding of low lying areas along the river as well as water spilling onto Liberty Avenue.

The Little Muskingum River near Bloomfield rose above its 16 foot bankfull level on the morning of May 7th, crested at 19.89 feet later that evening, and then returned to its banks just after midnight. While out of its banks, the river resulted in flooding on Route 26 near the intersection of Route 260 as well as flooding of nearby hay fields.

The Muskingum River near the town of Beverly rose above its 29 foot flood stage during the late morning hours of May 7th. The river crested just after noon and returned to its banks before the evening time frame. Primarily low lying areas adjacent to the river were impacted by the flooding, but a few homes and camp sites were impacted by high water as well.

Duck Creek at Macksburg rose above its 13 foot bankfull level just after midnight on May 7th. It remained out of its banks until the early morning hours of May 8th, cresting at 14.44 feet. This resulted in flooding along State Route 81 near Main Street and Broad Street. Surrounding low lying fields and campgrounds also flooded.

An EF1 tornado touched down on a hillside south of Little White Oak Road uprooting several trees. The tornado then traveled north across a newly mowed hay field with a convergent pattern evident in the mowed hay, then impacted a house and garage. The tornado tore off a large section of the roof of the home and destroyed the adjacent garage. Residents of the home witnessed the tornado as it was moving across the hay field toward the house and were able to take shelter. The tornado caused additional tree damage as it continued north up a ridge and then onto Cub Run Road.
Flash floding occurred in several areas along 8th Street Road (Route 152) from Lavalette to the Cabell County line with water in several houses.

Significant flash flooding occurred in Cabell County. The hardest hit area was the Enslow Park area where over 100 homes and many vehicles were inundated as Fourpole Creek flooded.  Some vehicles were swept away.  Route 10 was closed due to flash flooding near Huntinton High School, Route 60 was impassable at the East Mall Road intersection in Barboursville, and flood waters entered Davis Creek Elementary School.  A 63 year old man drowned in flood waters along Kilgore Creek Road in Milton.  The man was working on a farm tractor and high water swept him away.

Flash flooding occurred throughout the county.  Route 34 was impassable near City Park.  High water flowed across Route 817 in multiple locations in Winfield and several neighborhoods also had high water across roads.  A water rescue took place in Poca.

Widespread flash flooding occurred in Roane County.  In Newton, high water affected the EMS Substation and the road leading to the station was impassable.  Route 52 in Looneville was impassable.  Amma Road was was impassable and multiple structures along the road were flooded.  In Spencer, severel feet of water covered the intersection of Front Street and Market Street.

Local businesses and schools closed from the Christmas holiday remained closed through the end of the calendar year due to over 6,000 customers were without water, taking over a week for restoration. Over 75% of the county was without water for a prolonged period of time. Most of the water tanks in Beckley were drained over the Christmas holiday due to customer water line breaks and fire suppression systems freezing and busting from the extreme cold. Several businesses reported losing over 2 million gallons of water and residential lines leaked over 300,000 gallons of water in the Beckley area.

Water issues began on the evening of Christmas as extreme cold temperatures froze the water lines in the county. The Public Service District (PSD) that provides for Wayne County observed their entire water system go dry due to a chain reaction of issues. The Public Service Districts nearby, Kermit PSD and Mingo PSD in Mingo County, which is typically how Wayne County receives their water supply, failed due to ice jams along the local rivers. Once the water plants were restored, multiple leaks were discovered in their lines, which once again cut off water from reaching Wayne County. Most of these leaks were from main line shifts and breaks and burst water lines underneath private residences. ||Until lines could be restored after the Christmas holiday, county residents were under a boil water advisory. Residents in the county remained within a boil water advisory well into the new year as the restoration process continued.

In Hamlin, the gage along the Mud River observed a rise above the river's 13 foot bankfull level on the afternoon of February 16th. The river crested at 15.29 feet just before sunrise on the 17th and did not return to its banks until the early morning hours of February 18th. During this prolonged period of being out of its banks, the river caused flooding along sections of Upper Mud River Road as well as some homes along and near the Mud River. Sections of Route 7 between Myra and Hamlin, and sections of Route 3 on either side of Hamlin, also flooded. The ball fields near Lincoln County High School were under water during this time as well.

The Tug Fork in Williamson rose above its 27 foot flood stage late in the afternoon on February 17th. The river crested at 28.7 feet later that evening and returned to its banks a few hours after midnight on the 18th. The water treatment plant in Williamson closed its flood gate to help prevent water from the river to spill into the area until the floodwaters receded.

Shortly after midnight on February 17th, the Cranes Nest River in Clintwood rose above its 11 foot bankfull level. The river remained its banks through the late morning hours that day, cresting at 12.09 feet in the process. This resulted in minor flooding along low spots on Cranes Nest River Camp road leading up to the campground.

The Pound River in Norland rose above its 8 foot bankfull level around dawn on the morning of February 17th. The tornado caused considerable and significant tree damage with several large hardwood trees snapped and uprooted. A home was severely damaged when the roof was blown off, and other homes also suffered at least minor damage. Several barns and outbuildings were destroyed. The tornado then crossed the ridge between Long Branch Road and Jacks Fork Road and turned east, skipping along the ridgetops causing additional tree damage before lifting.

An EF1 tornado skipped along a path of straight-line wind damage likely beginning along Daniels Fork Road near the town of Westwood. The tornado then continued across State Route 5, moving eastward and crossing Rose Road and then ending at the top of the hill after crossing Pine Street. ||The most significant damage occurred along Rose Road. A single-wide trailer was flipped over, a section of a home was broken off from the rest of the structure and moved several feet, and several other homes and structures were significantly damaged.

A tornado formed along Erwin Hollow Road where several hardwood trees were snapped and uprooted. The tornado then moved northeast over a thick forest of mixed pine and hardwood trees between Erwin Hollow Road and Roberts Road where drone footage showed an extensive area of leveled hardwood trees and EF2 intensity was obtained. The drone footage and ground surveys then showed that the tornado weakened and the path became intermittent as it crossed Roberts Road, where a house was damaged when a tree fell on it. The last damage was noted along Oakland Road where several large pine trees were uprooted or snapped.

An EF1 tornado with maximum winds of 105 miles per hour began in the vicinity of Timber Ridge Lake in a rural area of northeast Lawrence County. There was a concentrated swath of significant hardwood tree damage observed along Scottown-Lecta Road just southeast of Timber Ridge Lake, with several large hardwoods either snapped or uprooted. This damage was consistent with a converging tornadic damage signature. ||Due to the rural area with which the tornado crossed and lack of a road network within the theoretical path, where the tornado first touched down and eventually lifted is unknown. In addition, this tornado may be an extension of the one which was observed in Aid.

An EF1 tornado began near Aid on Oak Ridge Road and traveled northeastward through mostly pastureland, knocking down a few trees on the north edge of the path and where it crossed Symmes Creek. The tornado continued northeast, blowing the roof off of two homes and another structure, as well as rolled a travel trailer near where it crossed State Route 141. The last noted damage was some tin panels that were blown upward on a barn roof shortly after the tornado crossed State Route 141. Some minor damage, not likely associated with the tornado occurred at the Symmes Valley High School.||An EMS employee stationed at the nearby Lawrence County EMS Station 5 witnessed the tornado as it traveled across the field in front of the station.

A broken path of damage was observed during a storm survey, beginning near the intersection of State Street and Shirkey Street to the Fairland West Elementary School. Little to no convergence was noted in the debris along the damage path, consistent with a microburst. The north wall of the Proctorville Fire Department, built of unreinforced concrete block, was destroyed, with the roof completely removed from the rear portion of the structure. The roof at the Fairland West Elementary School was also partially removed.

An EF2 tornado with maximum winds of 115 miles per hour followed a track of about 8 miles, extending from Cross Lanes to just south of the community of Wallace. This was a non-continuous path with three notable damage locations. Significant converging tree damage was observed along Hidden Pines Lane in Cross Lanes, where several large and unhealthy softwood trees were snapped at their bases along with uprooting of many large hardwood trees. Minor damage to homes were noted adjacent to this location along Hidden Cove.||The next area of significant tree convergence was observed along a narrow stretch of the 5000 block of Rock Fork Road, near Tyler Mountain Memory Gardens, where a utility pole was snapped at the base along with several uprooted mixed hardwood and softwood trees. This damage extended to a subdivision on Lynn Oak Drive where several large softwood and hardwood trees were either snapped or uprooted. One large hardwood tree fell onto a home in Cross Lanes, which resulted in significant damage to the second story. A local resident's john boat and camper were also flipped over and crushed by large trees in this area.||The final location where damage was noted occurred just south of the community of Wallace along the 4000 block of Sissonville Drive and Whittington Road. This was where several large softwood trees were either snapped or uprooted. In addition, sporadic tree damage was noted just south of the overall track, resulting from straight-line winds.

A short, but non-continuous, tornado path was observed with scattered tree damage behind a few homes west of the town of Quick. Significant converging tree damage was observed along the 7000 block of Quick Road just east of the town of Quick. Two mobile homes were destroyed at this location, with a roof uplifted and exterior wall damage. In addition, there was a utility pole that was snapped at the base.

An EF1 tornado with maximum winds of 100 miles per hour began in the St. Albans Park, where significant uprooting trees oriented in a north-northeast direction was observed along City Park Drive. On the adjacent side of the road there was a mixture of hard and softwood trees that were either uprooted or snapped, oriented in a southeast direction indicating a clear converging damage swath. Based on a combination of drone footage and ground surveys, it was determined that the tornado skipped eastward, embedded in a larger swath of straight-line wind damage, from St. Albans to Jefferson, before crossing over the Kanawha River into Dunbar, and finally ending in the Roxalana area. This was a non-continuous path with several noted areas of concentrated damage.||In St. Albans, several homes just west of Cunningham Memorial Park were damaged from fallen hardwood and softwood trees of decent size and health. One home was missing a section of wall on the east side of the structure. Multiple homes in the area of Hughes Drive, Lotus Road, and Squires Drive received damage from mixed hardwood and softwood trees that had fallen. Some of the trees were rather large and healthy.||In Jefferson, several trees of mixed hardwood and softwood along MacCorckle Avenue, Kanawha Terrace, Hampshire Drive, and Campbell Lane were uprooted or snapped with some falling on homes. Drone footage showed a path of convergent tree damage descending a hill and crossing Route 60, close to where a roof of a home was blown off. ||After crossing the river over to Dunbar, several trees around Dutch Hollow, Grandview, and into Roxalana Road were either snapped or uprooted with some siding and shingle damage noted to several homes and apartment buildings. A large billboard on Fairlawn Avenue, next to a restaurant and Interstate 64, was knocked over onto a car.

A tornado touched down in the Kanawha State Forest near the Pigeon Roost Trail, then skipped along an intermittent path eastward to the Hernshaw community. Significant tree damage was noted between Hernshaw and Marmet, with the most destructive being the top roof of a home being blown off, an RV that was rolled, and additional structure damage in and around Hernshaw. The tornado dissipated before reaching the I-64 corridor.
A short-lived tornado snapped and uprooted trees in a distinct path down a hillside into the valley in the Ronda community near Cabin Creek. A few homes suffered roof damage along Ronda Road.

A tornado, essentially a strong eddy at the end of a microburst, occurred along 5th Street Road near the Wayne/Cabell County line. More substantial damage occurred after the tornado crossed firmly into Cabell County, but structural damage along 5th Street Road was noted close to where the tornado touched down.

A quick tornado feeding off of a microburst crossed into Cabell County from Wayne County, producing sporadic straight-line wind damage from the Huntington Airport eastward to Harvey Road. From drone footage, it was apparent that this microburst descended into the north/south oriented valley at 5th Street Road near Woodhaven Drive. Tree and structural damage in this valley showed strong rotation with damage consistent with an EF1 tornado. Several structures were damaged or destroyed and extensive tree damage occurred. The tornado climbed the ridge to the east of 5th Street Road and dissipated.

An EF1 tornado with maximum winds of 105 miles per hour endured a track of about 4 miles, extending from just south of Route 2 near the Guyandotte River to just west of the Barboursville Mall. This was a non-continuous track with several notable damage locations.||A narrow concentrated area of hardwood tree damage was noted on a hilltop along Viewpoint Lane. Several of the trees were either snapped or uprooted in a converging pattern and continued southeast along Estate Drive.||Significant mixed hardwood and softwood tree damage was observed along Guyan River Road with most of the intense damage occurring along the banks of the Guyandotte River. Numerous large hardwood and softwood trees were either snapped or uprooted. Damage to a mobile home occurred due to a large fallen tree. In addition, damage to the roof of an apartment complex on the other side of the river on Beech Drive occurred from a fallen tree. This section of the track is where the maximum winds are believed to have occurred.||The tornado path continued eastward with a distinct damage swath of hardwood trees noted along Merritts Creek Road. Large hardwood trees were either snapped or uprooted in a converging pattern. A small mobile office unit was blown in the opposite direction of the orientation of the tree damage. From here, the tornado reached its maximum width of 200 yards as it entered into a valley. Tree damage continued east up the ridgetop along Big Ben Bowen Highway before ending along Wildcat Road. The tornado is believed to have lifted before reaching the Barboursville Mall, which is supported by archived radar images. ||This tornado, as with many of the others on this day, stayed mainly in the treetops with little in the way of property damage observed.||Outside of the tornado path, rear flank downdraft wind damage occurred east and southeast of the tornado, where a concrete block wall attached to the exterior of the mall was blown apart to the northeast. In addition, part of the roof of a business just east of the mall was lifted and blown to the northeast as well. Finally, scattered tree damage was observed on both sides of Interstate 64 east of the mall, with a general orientation to the northeast.

An EF1 tornado touched down south of Eleanor to Bancroft, with a non-continuous path and maximum winds of 90 miles per hour. Initial damage was observed along Hurricane Creek Road, just north of the intersection with Sugar Camp Road south of Fraziers Bottom.||Scattered tree damage was observed, mainly large limbs of hardwood trees with a few uprooted trees noted as well. There was a slight converging signature observed in this area. More significant hardwood tree damage was observed along State Route 34 south of Winfield with a concentrated area of hardwoods either snapped or uprooted with a more pronounced tornadic damage signature. ||Additionally, concentrated tree damage occurred along State Route 817 in the Shawnee Estates area across from Bancroft. Here, a narrow damage swath of several mixed hardwood and softwood trees were either snapped or uprooted, which continued eastward along Cannery Lane. A converging damage path was noted.||The tornado appeared to be in the treetops with only minor property damage observed. The tornado lifted just after crossing the Kanawha River.

An EF0 tornado with maximum winds of 80 miles per hour was discovered in the Buffalo area. Concentrated tree damage was observed along the side of a ridge along the east side of Railroad Avenue with several large hardwood trees uprooted in a north-northeast orientation, showing a slight converging signature. This signature became more apparent to the northeast along Cross Creek Road where several mixed softwood and hardwood trees were observed either uprooted or snapped. The tornado appeared to stay in the treetops with no property damage observed. The tornado quickly lifted along Cross Creek Road.

An EF1 tornado with maximum winds of 95 miles per hour first touched down along Hannan Trace Road about 3 miles northeast of Crown City. Several large hardwood trees were observed uprooted in a converging pattern within a narrow ravine at the 1650 block of Hannan Trace Road. This damage extended northeastward out of the ravine and onto the nearby hillside where some damage to barns occurred from fallen trees.||In addition, the roof and exterior walls of a wood frame commercial warehouse were blown off to the south of the path along Hannan Trace Road. Given the location of this particular damage and orientation, this likely occurred from rear flank downdraft winds. ||The exact start and end path to the tornado is unknown given the rural area with which it occurred and lack of a road network within the theoretical damage track.

A broken path of damage was noted on the Kentucky side of the tornado track, beginning at the Riverview Cemetery west of Greenup. Additional damage occurred on Seaton Avenue near South 5th Street and in the Greenup Fairgrounds, where a few buildings suffered roof damage and a large tree fell onto another building. The tornado then likely tracked along the Ohio River before intersecting land again on the Kentucky side and causing roof and tree damage to several homes along Calumet Drive.

A tornado that began in Greenup County, Kentucky finally crossed the Ohio River and impacted a campground on the Ohio side at Hanging Rock. More significant damage was noted here as several travel trailers were overturned, the roof was blown off of the Laidback Bar, and significant tree damage was noted in the adjacent camping area. Drone footage showed campers tossed in a counter-clockwise motion and some convergence in the tree damage. A salt storage dome was also destroyed in this area, causing significant injury to an employee.||The tornado continued to track eastward, damaging a few homes and damaging the roof and ballfields at Ironton Middle School. The tornado weakened but continued to cause some sporadic damage to homes all the way to the Storms Creek Flood Wall.
Multiple areas of downed trees were observed throughout the county.
Trees and power lines were blown down on Lowman Drive and Leighwood Drive.
A long swath of uprooted and snapped trees were observed along Southern Hills Drive. Several homes suffered damage from the fallen trees.

Measured on a Davis Weather Station mounted on the roof of the Boyd County Emergency Operations Center. Several buildings in the Industrial Park suffered damage to their roofs and their garage doors were blown in.
A healthy seventy foot pine tree fell onto a home near Cannonsburg along KY 180.
Numerous trees were blown down on Oakmont Manor.

Widespread tree and power line damage was observed in the Proctorville area. Multiple structures suffered damage due to downed trees and strong wind gusts. A truck was overturned on the Proctorville Bridge.

Damage consistent with a microburst occurred along Wilson Creek. Several trees were uprooted or snapped. A roof was also blown off of a nearby house.

Trees and power lines were blown down all over Huntington. A tractor trailer was flipped to its side on the 31st Bridge.

In the town of Cherry, several structures observed damage and a tree was blown down onto a house.

Multiple sheet metal roofs were damaged in Ravenswood.
In Shinnston, multiple trees were uprooted.

A storage shed was dislodged and blown across the street near Ansted.
A person was trapped inside a damaged structure along Bella Vista Drive.
Several trees were blown down around Montgomery.
Several trees were snapped on the hillside along US 60.
Damaged trees were observed along US 60.

A microburst with maximum winds of 100 miles per hour in the communities of Jodie and Swiss along the Nicholas and Fayette County line. Notable significant damage was first observed along Jodie Road where large mixed hardwood and softwood trees were either uprooted or snapped. This damage extended along the banks of the Gauley River and up the slopes of the adjacent hillsides. In addition, a roof was blown off of a home along with an attached car port from a different home. The tree damage continued northeast, crossing State Route 39, and ended up a narrow ravine on the north side of the road. It is here where numerous large hardwood trees were uprooted in a general northeast direction.||While there were isolated signs of converging tree damage, likely from steep terrain induced wind patterns, the overwhelming evidence indicated the occurrence of a microburst. This conclusion was further supported by radar interrogation.
Several trees were blown down and blocked Selbyville Road near Newlon.
A tree was blown down, blocking Back Mountain Road.
Trees were blown down on Mountain Quest Lane near Frost.
Widespread tree damage was observed in the Bickmore community.
Lines of trees knocked down onto both sides of Selbyville Road.
A tree was blown down across Horseshoe Road near the Philip Barbour High School.
A metal roof was removed off of a house with nearby power lines also down near the Dorothy community.
A tree was blown down and blocking Sherwood Road near Price Hill.
Trees and power lines were blown down at Horse Creek Road and Coal River Road.
Trees were blown down between Horse Creek Road and Pettry Bottom Road.
Multiple trees were down in the Runa community.
Part of a roof was blown off with a window broken out in Richwood.
Several large limbs fell onto a home in Summersville.
Several trees, mostly pine, were uprooted or snapped on Dove Lane and Elkhorn Lane. One tree fell onto a house, damaging the roof. Damage was indicative of a microburst.
A small area with multiple uprooted hardwood trees were observed near the intersection of Leivasy Road and Odell Road, indicative of a microburst.
A roughly 500 yard long swath of uprooted trees was observed along Laurel Creek and Saxman Road. Tree damage was divergent, indicative of microburst winds blowing oddly from south to north.
Sporadic tree damage was observed along Snow Hill Road with minor roof damage to a home.

Areas of trees were blown down between Chapmanville and Logan.

In Hamlin, several structures were damaged along with multiple downed trees around town and up Route 34 toward Hurricane.
Tree damage consistent with a microburst observed on a ridgetop along Sand Gap Road.
Path of tree damage consistent with a microburst occurred along Route 214 between Yawkey and Sumerco Hill.
A small area of uprooted trees were observed at the intersection of Snow Hill Road and Leivasy Road, indicative of a microburst.
A funnel cloud was spotted near Marietta.
A large tree was blown down at the State Garage, blocking part of State Route 669 near the Muskingum County line. Another tree was downed outside the town of Crooksville.
One tree was blown down along State Route 427 outside of New Straitsville.
One tree was blown down, completely blocking County Road 7 outside of Ironton.
A tree was blown down onto Coon Branch Road, blocking one lane of traffic.

Downed trees and lines resulted in power outages on Ranchland Lane.

A pine tree, about 12 to 15 inches in diameter, was downed and blocked Shawnee Drive near the local apartment buildings.

Numerous areas of downed trees were observed in South Charleston, including at Ridge Drive, Kirby Street, and Richmond Road. The roof of a deck also collapsed at a home in South Charleston.
Several power poles with lines were blown down along US-50 outside the town of Salem.
A big and healthy tree fell down and blocked all lanes of Grassy Run Road and also taking down a telephone line. A few other trees were blown down nearby.
High water was observed along State Route 13 just north of New Lexington.
State Route 328 was closed in both directions near State Route 56 due to flooding. In McArthur, vehicles became stuck in high water along Goose Creek Road.
Street flooding was observed in downtown Athens.
Multiple road closures were observed across Vinton County as a result of flooding. These included State Route 56, State Route 278, and US 50.
Power lines were blown down in a Parkersburg neighborhood. A tree was also blown down on Montgomery Hill Road.
Trees were blown down across Willbrook Drive near Vienna.
A tree was blown down across Deerwalk Highway.
Trees and power lines were blown down in North Hills.

A metal carport roof was blown off on Centerville Road in Rock Cave.
Numerous trees were blown down in the Buckhannon area. A dumpster was flipped over and a roof was ripped off of a building.
A barn was damaged near Bridge Run Road outside of Buckhannon.
Several trees were snapped and uprooted near Maplewood. Power poles were snapped and lines blown down. A nearby home suffered roof damage and blown off shingles.

A brief EF1 tornado occurred east of Parkersburg on the evening of May 9th. Initial concentrated tree damage north of Rising Sun Ridge Road was found during the storm survey. There were hardwood trees observed uprooted with additional large branches down in a converging pattern.||The damage continued southeast to a small section of Jericho Road. Here, a narrow swath of large mixed hardwood and softwood trees were observed either uprooted or snapped close to their bases. In addition, a mobile home and barn were flipped over. There was one minor injury, as a person was inside the mobile home at the time it flipped over. There was a clear converging damage pattern noted here. Tree damage continued southeast to the end of Whitlatch Lane where large mixed hardwood and softwood trees were uprooted or snapped in a converging pattern. The highest rated damage occurred at these locations and served as the basis for the EF1 rating.||The tornado continued southeast to Ralston Hill Road and weakened, as only a few trees were uprooted or snapped with primarily large branches down. The tornado lifted along the southern end of State Route 31, just north of State Highway 50. A few trees were uprooted with large branches down along with an RV that was rolled over.
One tree and power line was blown down near Chesapeake.
A tree was blown down, blocking both lanes of State Route 522 in Lisman.
A tree was blown down, which blocked both lanes of County Road 210.
Trees were blown down outside the town of South Shore.
Near McClure, a tree was blown down along Carter Stanley Highway. Another tree was downed along Doe Branch in Haysi.
A tree was blown down along Rockhouse Road outside of Clintwood.
A portion of a roof was blown off of a home in Raceland with trees blown down.
A tree was blown down at the intersection of Red Devil Lane and Seaton Drive in Russel.
Near the town of South Shore, a tree was blown down onto power lines, causing local power outages.
A tree was downed at Caroline Road and Greenup Avenue in Raceland.
In Raceland, a tree was blown down onto a local road.
In Grahamsville, a tree was blown down onto power lines, causing numerous local power outages.

Multiple trees were blown down in the town of Jackson, some of which fell onto vehicles. Structural damage to commercial and residential buildings were observed, including roof damage in the southern part of the city along and near Route 93, just north of Route 124.

Numerous areas of damage were observed along Route 124 in the vicinity of a hospital south of the town of Jackson. The damage included numerous downed trees and power lines, sections of roofs peeled off, and semi-trucks that were flipped over.

A tornado touched down near Mount Zion Road where some minor tree damage occurred and swirl patterns were found in a hay field. The tornado tracked northeastward across State Route 139 where tree damage occurred and an outbuilding was damaged. It continued to skip along causing intermittent tree damage in neighborhoods north of State Route 32. The tornado knocked a tree down onto a vehicle at Hope Haven School then snapped or uprooted several trees, some onto vehicles, behind Rowdy's Smokehouse. This is where the tornado reached maximum EF1 intensity with winds estimated up to 90 miles per hour. ||The tornado then crossed Main Street, ripped a portion of the roof of of the Tractor Supply building, flipped over a parked semi trailer in the parking lot and then caused roof damage to buildings in the Senior Village. Some minor tree damage was then noted to the east of US-35 along Pattonsville Road where the tornado path ended.||This was the 8th known tornado in Jackson County and the 2nd so far this year.
Flooding occurred along Crim Avenue. Water entered one building in Belington.
A vehicle became stuck in high water on Core Road.

The Ohio River at the Belleville Lock rose above flood stage on the morning of April 3rd and continued to rise to a crest of 41.9 feet a few days later, on the morning of the 5th. The river then eased back below flood stage during the early morning hours of April 7th. This extended period of the river out of its banks resulted flooding of local roads on the West Virginia side of the river.
Hail as big as quarters fell.

The Ohio River at Parkersburg rose above flood stage on the afternoon of April 3rd, then continued to rise to a crest of around 40.1 feet the morning of the 5th. The river then fell back below flood stage the afternoon of April 6th. This extensive amount of time above flood stage resulted in flooding of several homes in the Happy Valley and Point Drive areas near Parkersburg as well as sections of Vienna.

The Ohio River at Point Pleasant rose above its 40 foot flood stage on the morning of April 4th, then reached a crest of around 44.7 feet on the morning of the 6th. The river then receded below flood stage the evening of April 7th. During this extended period of time with the river out of its banks, numerous local roads in the area observed high water issues, including Route 21 and Route 33. Homes at the end of 2nd Street outside of the flood wall in Point Pleasant also experienced minor flooding.

The Ohio River at Racine Lock rose above flood stage on the night of April 3rd, then reached a crest of around 46.4 feet on the night of the 5th. The river gradually receded below flood stage again the following morning. While in flood, West Virginia Route 62 at Tombleson Creek flooded and portions just below the Racine Lock at West Creek flooded as well.

The Middle Fork Tygart Valley River at Audra rose just above its bankfull level on the afternoon of April 3rd. The river crested to feet and then returned to its banks later that evening. This caused minor flooding at the campground in Audra State Park and the roadways in the extreme low-lying areas of the park.

The Tygart Valley River at Belington rose above its bankfull level on the afternoon of April 3rd. The river continued to rise to a crest of 16.4 feet that night and then returned below bankfull level the next morning. This resulted in high water spilling onto Talbott Road and Wasbash Road.

Shepards White Oak Creek flooded County Route 115, which is also known as Upcreek Road.  The headwater areas of White Oak and Kyger Creeks flooded portions of Route 554.  ||No structures were affected and nobody drove their vehicles into the high water.

The Tygart Valley River at Philippi rose above its 19 foot flood stage on the evening of April 3rd. The river continued to rise to a crest of around 19.7 feet that night and then returned below flood stage the next morning. This resulted in minor flooding at the intersection of US Route 119 and Truck Route 250, as well as at Sycamore Street and Beech Avenue in Philippi.
Trees were blown down.

The Middle Fork Tygart Valley River at Ellamore rose above its 13 foot bankfull level on the afternoon of April 3rd. The river continued to rise to a crest of around 14.8 feet and returned to its banks the same evening. Portions of County Route 28 near the Randolph/Upshur County line observed high water issues while the river was out of its banks.

In Mill Creek, the Tygart Valley River rose out of its banks on the afternoon of April 3rd. The river crested around 12.2 feet that afternoon, then returned below its bankfull level on the night of the 4th. While the river was out of its banks, County Route 39 heading out of town observed flooding.

The Olive Hill gauge on Tygarts Creek rose above its bankfull level shortly after midnight on April 3rd. The creek crested to around 11.4 feet a couple of hours later and returned to its banks before sunrise. As a result of the creek rising out of its banks, sections of Biggs Bridge Road adjacent to the creek flooded.

The Ohio River gauge at Ashland rose above flood stage on the morning of April 6th, crested to around 52 feet that evening, and then fell back below flood stage early the next morning. Minor flooding of low lying areas in the town of Ashland occurred during this time due to backwater from the draining creeks. The Catlettsburg flood gate at 15th and Center Street was also closed while the river was above its flood stage.
Fraziers Branch exceeded its banks and caused flooding along Brown Pond Road.
Water and debris spread over sections of Cub Run Road.
Big Lost Creek Road was closed due to flooding between mile markers 8 and 10.
State Route 2 was blocked due to flooding near the 6.4 mile marker.
South Branch of Wolf Creek exceeded its banks and caused flooding along several roads in the area.

The Macksburg gauge on the West Fork Duck Creek rose above its bankfull level on the evening of April 2nd, then continued to rise to a crest of around 14.9 feet the following evening. Waters thereafter slowly receded and returned below bankfull just before sunrise on the 4th. The campground next to the gauge flooded during this time, as did parts of Broad Street and Main Street.

The Bloomfield gauge on the Little Muskingum River rose above bankfull level on the night of April 2nd. The river crested around 24 feet the following afternoon, and then returned to its banks during the early morning hours of April 4th. In addition to high water issues that arose along Route 26 and Route 260, Bloomfield Church Road near the Little Muskingum River bridge flooded.

The Muskingum River at Beverly rose above its flood stage on the evening of April 2nd. The river crested to around 34.7 feet the following morning and then returned below flood stage on the morning of the 4th. While the river spilled out of its banks, several areas near the river flooded, as did farmland and several sections of Route 60.

The Muskingum River gauge at McConnelsville rose above its flood stage on the afternoon of April 2nd. The river eventually crested to around 13 feet the next morning, and then returned below flood stage the morning of the 4th. Several homes and businesses in the McConnelsville observed minor flooding during this time, in addition to high water issues that arose on State Route 376 and Route 669.

The Duck Creek at Whipple rose above its bankfull level of 12 feet shortly after midnight on April 3rd. The creek crested around 15.8 feet during the afternoon and returned to its banks the next morning. Flooding occurred along sections of Route 821, the intersection of Kohl Road and Whipple Run Road, Route 16 near Stanleyville, and on agricultural fields in the vicinity of the creek.

The Ohio River at the Marietta Pumphouse rose above flood stage on the morning of April 3rd and continued to rise to a crest of around 40.1 feet on the morning of the 5th. The river then fell back below flood stage on the afternoon of April 6th. ||While the river was risen, major flooding occurred in the Marietta area. Wayne Street at Eighth Street, Greene Street at Second, Seventh and Pike Streets, Front Street at Monroe Street and at the Armory, Pennsylvania Avenue at Linwood Street and at Eton Street, Second Street at Butler Street, and Scammel Street at Second and Third Streets all flooded. On the West Side of Marietta, Harmar Street at Maple and Pearl Streets, and Market Street at Fort Square also flooded.

The Ohio River at Pomeroy rose above its flood stage on the afternoon of April 4th, then continued to rise to a crest of around 48 feet on the afternoon of the 5th. The river then fell back below flood stage the night of April 6th. Businesses that reside along the river flooded during this time, as did several parking lots and the river amphitheater.
Several large tree branches were blown down.

The Ohio River gauge at Willow Island Lock rose above its flood stage on the morning of April 3rd, then reached a crest of around 41.3 feet the morning of the 5th. The river then receded below flood stage the next morning. With the river spilling out of its banks, water inundated Ohio Route 7 in the Reno area. Ohio State Route 7, Township Road 443, and Township Road 19 at Newell Run and Lenards Landing flooded.||During the time the river was out of its banks, a 42 year old man perished after attempting to drive through the floodwaters on State Route 7 just north of Archer Fork Road.

In the town of Aid, Symmes Creek rose above its bankfull level on the afternoon of April 3rd, then continued to rise to a crest of around 19.8 feet that night. The creek receded below bankfull again the next morning. Low lying sections of Ohio Route 378 and Ohio Route 217 flooded during the time the creek was out of its banks.

The Shade River at Chester rose above its bankfull level on the night of April 2nd. The river made an initial crest the next day, then rose again to a final crest near 20.8 feet shortly after midnight on the 4th. Waters receded from there and returned to its banks on the afternoon of the 4th. Several local roads near the gauge observed flooding during this time, including Scout Camp Road.

The Ohio River at Ashland rose above flood stage shortly after midnight on the 15th of April. The river continued to rise to a crest of around 52 feet later that morning and then eased back below flood stage that evening. Minor flooding of roads in low lying areas near Catlettsburg occurred during the time the Ohio River was above its flood stage.

The Little Muskingum River at Bloomfield exceeded its bankfull level on the evening of April 11th. The river continued to rise to a crest of around 21.5 feet the next morning and then returned to its banks once again on the evening of the 12th. Portions of Route 26 near the intersection of Route 260 observed high water issues while the river was out of its banks.

Duck Creek below Whipple rose above its bankfull level early in the morning on April 12th. The creek crested around 13.4 feet late that morning and then returned to its banks that night. While the creek was out of its banks, the intersection of Kohl Road and Whipple Run Road flooded due to backwater flooding of Whipple Run.

The Shade River near Chester rose above its bankfull level on the morning of April 12th. After cresting around 17.9 feet that evening, waters receded below bankfull early the next morning. A few low lying spots along Scout Camp Road near the Sugar Run Creek bridge flooded as a result of the river spilling out of its banks.

The Ohio River at Marietta exceeded its flood stage on the night of April 13th and continued to rise to a crest of around 37.9 feet overnight. After cresting, the river slowly fell and returned below flood stage early on the 15th. Several local roads in Marietta flooded as a result during this time, including Hart Street, Jefferson Street, and Pike Street.

The gauge along the Ohio River at Pomeroy indicated a rise above flood stage on the night of April 13th. The river crested around 47 feet the next afternoon and then fell back below flood stage late in the morning on the 15th. While above flood stage, parking lots in Pomeroy and the river amphitheater flooded, as well as secondary roads due to backwater.

The Ohio River at Willow Island Lock exceeded its flood stage during the pre-dawn hours on the 13th of April. The river continued to rise to a crest of around 38.8 feet early on the 14th, then fell below flood stage later that night. Ohio State 7, Township Road 443, and Township Road 19 at Newell Run and Lenards Landing flooded while the river spilled out of its banks.

Crab Orchard Creek flooded Route 16.  Little Whitestick Creek aided in causing severe street flooding in Beckley near the intersection of Route 16 and Kanawha Street.  Water was 2 feet deep, flooding vehicles.  Elsewhere in town, numerous basements were flooded.  Airport Road was flooded by Brammer Branch.
Roads in Kumbrabow State Forest were impassible by flooding of the headwater feeder runs into Mill Creek.

Little Tygart Creek at Mineral Wells climbed above its 11 foot bankfull level on the afternoon of April 12th, then continued to rise to a crest of around 15.3 feet the following evening. Backwater from of the Ohio River sustained flooding along Little Tygart Creek until the morning of the 15th. This level of flooding impacted most of Speedway Road and sections of Woodridge Drive and Dickens Drive. Flooding also reached a home on Mayo Drive above the intersection with Irene Lane.

Middle Island Creek at Little rose above its bankfull level on April 11th, just before midnight. The creek crested to around 20.1 feet on the evening of the 12th and then returned to its banks the next morning. Flooding reached private cabins and the access road near the Friendly Road bridge. Cabins and the bait house near the gauge also experienced flooding. Several primary and secondary roads flooded in low areas along Middle Island Creek and tributaries flowing into Middle Island Creek.

The Ohio River at Parkersburg rose above flood stage just after midnight on the 13th of April. The river reached a crest of around 38.5 feet early the next morning, then fell below flood stage before sunrise on the 15th. Several homes flooded in the Happy Valley and Point Drive areas near Parkersburg, along the Little Kanawha River. A few homes flooded on Annas Drive in Vienna, West Virginia, as well as Dave's Marina, Walnut Street, and Scott Avenue in Belpre, Ohio.

The Ohio River at Point Pleasant rose above flood stage early in the morning of April 13th.  After reaching a crest of around 43.8 feet early on the 15th, the river descended below flood stage the morning of April 16th. While the river was out of its banks, water spilled onto Route 21 at Eight Mile Creek above Ambrosia. Flooding also impacted Routes 30 and 62 near Rockcastle Creek and Ambrosia, Ohio Route 7 at Kyger Creek and Addison, Little Kyger Road and Blaville Road in Ohio, and low lying areas surrounding Point Pleasant.

The Ohio River at Racine Lock rose above its flood stage of 41 feet early in the morning of April 13th. After reaching a crest of around 44.6 feet on the afternoon of the 14th, the river returned below flood stage the next evening. West Virginia Route 62 flooded just below Racine Lock at West Creek due to the river spilling out of its banks. Sections of Ohio Route 124 and areas of Ravenswood also flooded.
Trees were blown down.
Penny size hail fell in Lynco and Matheny.

The Ohio River at Belleville Lock rose above its 35 foot flood stage on the evening of April 12th and then continued to rise to a crest of around 40.1 feet on the morning of the 14th. The river eventually receded below flood stage again the afternoon of April 15. While spilled out of its banks, Route 124 and sections of Ohio State Route 248 at Sand Hill were flooded.

Middle Island Creek near Middlebourne exceeded bankfull on the night of April 11th. The creek continued to rise to a crest of around 24.1 feet on the afternoon of the 12th, then fell returned to its banks again that night. Major flooding occurred along routes 18 and 24 on either side of Middlebourne. 4H camp buildings, county fairgrounds, and the agricultural field near the gauge flooded while the creek was out of its banks.

On the 11th, just before midnight, the Mud River exceeded its bankfull level near Griffithsville. The river reached a crest to around 12.4 feet a couple of hours later and then eased back below bankfull before sunrise on the 12th. Fields and low areas along the Middle Fork Mud River both upstream and downstream of the gauge flooded during the time the river was out of its banks.

Below the town of Mac Farlan, the South Fork Hughes River exceeded its bankfull level not long after midnight on the 12th. Waters rose to a crest of around 25.2 feet on the afternoon of the 12th and then fell back below bankfull that evening. Low sections of Oxbow Road below the gage flooded. Flooding also occurred in the agricultural field next to the river and just below the Staunton Turnpike bridge.

The river crested to around 25 feet that afternoon and then receded below flood stage again the same evening. Tygarts Creek above Olive Hill rose above its bankfull level of 10 feet during the pre-dawn hours of February 6th. The creek rose to a crest of 14.5 feet during the morning, then receded below bankfull around midday. While above its banks, the lower section of Chili Street and the American Legion building off Lawton Road flooded. Agricultural fields, Bond Hollow Road, and low sections of Biggs Bridge Road next to the creek also flooded.

Blaine Creek near Blaine exceeded a bankfull level of 17 feet on the morning of February 6th. The creek reached a crest of 20.3 feet that afternoon and then returned below bankfull around midnight. While the creek was out of its banks, portions of the Blaine Elementary School, low sections of Route 32, Blaine Community Park, and agricultural fields adjacent to the creek were all flooded.

The Little Sandy River at Grayson exceeded its flood stage of 21 feet on the morning of February 6th. The river crested around 24.4 feet that afternoon and then receded below flood stage again early the next morning. While the river spilled out of its banks, flooding of low spots on Route 773 and Jackson Road occurred. Additional flooding of buildings next to the gauge was observed, along with flooding in the Dixie Park area, along State Route 1910, and flooding of farmland and low spots in the vicinity of Grayson.

The Mud River north of Milton rose above its bankfull level of 19 feet on the morning of February 6th. The river rose to a crest of around 22.4 feet late that night, then receded below bankfull the afternoon of the 7th. This resulted in flooding on low spots along East Mud River Road and West Mud River Road.

The Mud River at Hamlin exceeded a bankfull level of 13 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The river reached a crest around 13.7 feet that night and then returned below bankfull the next morning. Sections of Route 3 in West Hamlin flooded as result. In addition, Peppermint Lane and surrounding fields in Myra and along the Mud River between Palermo and Hamlin flooded.

The Mud River near Griffithsville exceeded a bankfull level of 12 feet the morning of February 6th. The river reached a crest around 13.3 feet late that morning and then returned below bankfull during the evening. Fields and low areas along the Middle Fork Mud River flooded as a result.

Hurricane Creek near Hurricane exceeded a bankfull level of 17 feet the morning of February 6th. The creek reached a crest around 18.7 feet mid morning and then returned below bankfull that afternoon. While the creek was out of its banks, flooding occurred on low spots along Hurricane Creek Road and Peach Ridge Road.

Elk Twomile Creek at Charleston exceeded a bankfull level of 6.5 feet before daybreak on February 6th. The creek continued to rise to a crest of 8.3 feet and then returned below bankfull later the same morning. The Kanawha-Charleston Humane Association observed water reaching their overflow kennel space while the creek was out of its banks. Flooding also occurred at the intersection of Rutledge Road and Greenbrier Street in downtown Charleston, with water approaching several homes. Rutledge Road was impassable due to flooding.

Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek exceeded a bankfull level of 11 feet the morning of February 6th. The river continued to rise to a crest near 14.1 feet that afternoon, then receded below bankfull the following morning. One half to one foot of water went over Bradley Road at Right Fork of Mill Creek. On Channell Road, several homes were surrounded by water and one water rescue occurred.

The Shade River near Chester exceeded a bankfull level of 16 feet on the morning of February 6th. The river rose to a crest of around 18.7 feet that afternoon and then returned below bankfull the next morning. While the river was out of its banks, flooding occurred along low sections of Scout Camp Road near the gauge and on the Sugar Run Creek bridge. Agricultural fields and low-lying areas adjacent to the river also observed flooding.

Little Tygart Creek at Mineral Wells exceeded a bankfull level of 11 feet on the morning of February 6th. The creek rose to a crest around 11.5 feet that morning, then returned below bankfull in the afternoon. Portions of Irene Lane and low spots on Woodridge Golf Course flooded while the creek was out of its banks.

South Fork Hughes River below Macfarlan exceeded a bankfull level of 22 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The river crested around 22.1 feet during the afternoon and then returned below bankfull later that evening. This led to flooding of low sections of Oxbow Road and agricultural fields next to the river.

The Tygart Valley River at Dailey exceeded its flood stage of 14 feet on the evening of February 6th. The river crested around 14.5 feet that night and then returned below flood stage by midnight. While out of its banks, flooding occurred along Back Road, near the Georgetown Road bridge, and low lying areas near the river.

Williams River at Dyer exceeded a bankfull level of 10.5 feet on the morning of February 6th. The river reached a crest of around 11.9 feet that afternoon, then receded below bankfull by evening. This led to flooding of Forest Service Road 101 and sections of Williams River Road while out of its banks.

The Buckhannon River at Alton exceeded a bankfull level of 14 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The river crested around 14.3 feet and returned below bankfull later that afternoon. A few low lying areas near the Buckhannon River and Big Run Creek flooded as a result.

Middle Fork Tygart Valley River at Ellamore exceeded a bankfull level of 13 feet on the morning of February 6th. The river crested around 15.7 feet that afternoon, then returned below bankfull during the evening. While out of its banks, high water spilled onto County Route 28 for a period of time.

Middle Fork Tygart Valley River at Audra exceeded a bankfull level of 10 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The river crested around 10.4 feet during the afternoon and then returned below bankfull in the evening. Flooding occurred as a result at the campground and some low-lying areas within Audra State Park.

The Greenbrier River at Durbin exceeded a bankfull level of 7 feet on the morning of February 6th. The river crested around 7.9 feet in the afternoon and returned below bankfull that night. This resulted in minor flooding along local roads adjacent to the river.

Knapp Creek at Huntersville exceeded a bankfull level of 9 feet on the morning of February 6th. The creek reached a crest around 9.5 feet in the afternoon and returned below bankfull that evening. As a result of the creek rising out of its banks, flooding of farmland, fields, and outbuildings next to Knapp Creek and Browns Creek occurred. Knapp Creek also flooded Huntersville Road.

Middle Island Creek near Middlebourne exceeded a bankfull level of 16 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The creek crested around 16.2 feet and then returned below bankfull that night and resulted in flooding of fields, low and poor drainage areas along the creek.

The Buckhannon River at Buckhannon exceeded its flood stage of 23 feet on the evening of February 6th. The river crested around 24.3 feet that night and then returned below flood stage the next morning. Portions of Cleveland Avenue, Wood Street, Route 20, River Road, Vicksburg Road, and the intersection of Madison and Florida Streets experienced high water issues as a result of the river spilling out of its banks. Portions of Norvell Drive and some homes and low lying areas in and around Buckhannon also flooded due to backwater.

The Tygart Valley River at Belington exceeded its flood stage of 14 feet on the night of February 6th. The river crested around 16.3 feet the next morning and then returned below flood stage the night of the 7th. Flooding occurred on the small bridge along Willow Street, the intersection of Talbot and Wabash Roads, and some basements while the river was out of its banks.

The Little Kanawha River at Glenville exceeded its flood stage of 23 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The river crested near 25 feet that evening and then returned below flood stage the following afternoon. While the river was out of its banks, portions of Elm Street flooded, as well as portions of Brooklyn Drive and River Street. At one point, water reached the foundation of the hotel on Conrad Court next to the 1885 bridge.

The Elk River at Queen Shoals exceeded its flood stage of 19 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The river crested around 19.9 feet that night and then returned below flood stage early the next morning. Minor flooding of the North and South Clendenin boat ramp access parking lots occurred while the river was out of its banks.

The Greenbrier River at Marlinton exceeded its flood stage of 10 feet on the afternoon of February 6th. The river crested around just under 12 feet that night and then returned below flood stage by the next morning. While out of its banks, sections of 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Avenues in Marlinton, sections of 9th Street and Campbelltown, and low areas along the river all flooded. Knapp Creek also flooded Huntersville Road.

The Tygart Valley River at Mill Creek exceeded a bankfull level of 11 feet on the afternoon of January 31st. The creek crested around 13.4 feet that night and then receded below bankfull again the following afternoon. While out of its banks, flooding occurred along sections of County Route 39 near Mill Creek.

The Middle Fork Tygart Valley River at Ellamore exceeded a bankfull level of 13 feet the evening of January 31st. The river crested around 16.9 feet that night and then returned below bankfull the next morning. Sections of County Route 28 on the Randolph/Upshur County line adjacent to the river observed high water issues while the river was out of its banks.

The Dry Fork gage at Bradshaw exceeded a bankfull level of 10 feet on the evening of January 31. The river crested around 10.7 feet just after midnight on February 1st and then receded below bankfull during the late morning hours. While out of its banks, flooding occurred near homes along the river downstream of the gage.

The Little Kanawha River at Glenville crept above its flood stage of 23 feet on the night of January 31st. After cresting around 24.6 feet during the early morning hours of February 1st, the river returned below flood stage around daybreak. Some minor flooding on Elm Street, Brooklyn Drive, and River Street in Glenville occurred as a result of the river spilling out of its banks.

Knapp Creek at Huntersville exceeded a bankfull level of 9 feet on the night of January 31st. The creek crested around 9.2 feet a few minutes after midnight and then receded below bankfull again during the early morning hours of February 1st. Farmland, fields, and outbuildings adjacent to Knapp Creek and Browns Creek observed flooding while the creek was out of its banks.

The gage along Clear Fork River at Clear Fork exceeded a bankfull level of 11 feet on the evening of January 31st. The river crested around 11.1 feet and then receded below bankfull again that night. Portions of Charlie Hatfield Road observed high water issues while the river spilled out of its banks.

The Sand Run Creek exceeded a bankfull level of 6 feet on the afternoon of January 31st. The creek crested around 6.6 feet during the evening, then returned below bankfull that night. Low lying areas along Sand Run Creek experienced minor flooding during the time the creek was out of its banks.

The Middle Fork Tygart Valley River at Audra exceeded a bankfull level of 11 on feet the morning of January 31st. The river crept up to 11.11 feet just after midnight on February 1st, then receded below bankfull just before sunrise. Impacts observed in the midst of the river spilling out of its banks was some minor flooding of County Route 39 near the bridge.

The Tygart Valley River at Belington exceeded its flood stage of 14 feet on the night of January 31st. After cresting around 16.3 feet the next morning, the river returned below flood stage the morning on February 2nd. In downtown Belington, the Willow Street bridge and the intersection of Talbott and Wabash Roads flooded while the river was out of its banks. Around 8 am, a water rescue occurred at the intersection of Talbott and Wabash Roads in Belington. Between 11 am and Noon, another water rescue occurred in Junior near the intersection of West River Avenue and Fox Road.

The Tygart Valley River at Philippi exceeded its flood stage of 19 feet beginning on the night of January 31st. After cresting around 21.4 feet early the next morning, the river returned below flood stage on the evening of February 1st. While the river was out of its banks, flooding occurred on Chestnut Street, McCartney Street, Sycamore Street and Beech Avenue in downtown Philippi. The Vietnam Veterans Park and the intersection of US 119 and Truck Route 250 also flooded.

The river gage at the Buckhannon River in Buckhannon exceeded its flood stage of 23 feet around midnight on February 1st. After cresting near 25.2 feet later that morning, the river returned below flood stage that evening. Flooding was observed along several streets in downtown Buckhannon, as well as homes and businesses along the river.

Blaine Creek near Blaine exceeded a bankfull level of 17 feet on the morning of January 31st. The creek crested around 17.6 feet and then receded below bankfull again that night. Impacts while the creek was out of its banks included flooding along low sections of Route 32, the Blaine Community Park, and fields adjacent to the creek.

The Shade River near Chester exceeded a bankfull level of 16 feet on the morning of February 16th. Within the next couple of hours, rising waters submerged roads, impacted homes, and trapped residents in several locations. Floodwaters also rose halfway up the legacy bank building in Hurley. Impacted locations included Paw Paw Road, Rustic Road, McKracken Road, Guesses Fork Road, Hurley Road, Tree Top Road, Dan Branch Road, Lesters Fork Road, Race Fork Road, Cedar Branch Road, and Knox Creek Drive.
Significant flooding continued to impact numerous roadways and structures in Hurley and the surrounding areas. Two roads that became washed out during this event were Rustic and Thimble Roads.

Among the impacted roads were Bear Pen Creek Road, Cutter Creek Road, Coeburn Road, Pioneer Street, Jessee Street, Wave Drive, Short Street, and Power House Hollow Road.

Flooding became exacerbated by continued rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and many impassable roads in the vicinity of Clintwood, Haysi, Clinchco, Davenport, and Breaks, among others. After cresting near 19.7 feet that morning, the creek lowered to, and then hovered around, bankfull level through the afternoon. The creek slightly rose during the evening, but then receded back into its banks just after midnight on the morning of February 17. Impacts include flooding of low sections along Mose Asbury Road and the athletic fields at Twelvepole Valley Park.

The Mud River above Milton exceeded a bankfull level of 19 feet the afternoon of February 16. After cresting near 20.5 feet that night, the river lowered back into its banks the next morning. Impacts include flooding of several low spots along East Mud River Road and West Mud River Road.

The Mud River at Hamlin exceeded a bankfull level of 13 feet the morning of February 16. After cresting around 13.9 feet that afternoon, the river lowered back into its banks early the next morning. Impacts include flooding of sections of Route 3 in West Hamlin, ball fields near the high school bridge, Peppermint Lane and surrounding fields in Myra, and fields along the river between Palermo and Hamlin.

The Mud River near Griffithsville exceeded a bankfull level of 12 feet the night of February 15. After cresting near 13.1 feet overnight, the river lowered back into its banks the next morning. Impacts include flooding of fields and low areas along the Middle Fork Mud River.

Little Tygart Creek at Mineral Wells exceeded a bankfull level of 11 feet the morning of February 16. After cresting just over 11.2 feet, the creek returned to its banks later the same morning. Impacts include flooding of low sections of Irene Lane, and Woodridge Golf Course.

After an initial crest just shy of bankfull before daybreak, the river eventually exceeded bankfull that afternoon. A second crest, just under 19.1 feet, occurred before waters gradually eased back below bankfull during the evening.
