The river slowly receded and eventually fell back below flood stage the morning of the 17th. Around 1 am on the 16th, the City of Williamson notified the public that the flood gates would be shut. Outside of the flood walls, major flooding impacted the 2nd Avenue and Harvey Street Bridges, sections of Highway 292, several roads, and many homes and businesses in the Williamson and South Williamson areas.

The Tug Fork River at Kermit exceeded its flood stage of 38 feet the morning of February 16, then continued to rise to a crest around 51.2 feet just after midnight on the 17th. The river then receded and fell back below flood stage the night of the 17th. Major flooding impacted homes from Collier Street to Elm Street, and the commercial district south of the Virginia Avenue bridge in Kermit. In Warfield, most of the business district, homes on Hode Road, and the grocery store on Beauty Road flooded. In Lovely, most homes and businesses between Riverfront Road and the river flooded.

The Guyandotte River at Branchland exceeded its flood stage of 30 feet the morning of February 16, then continued to rise to a crest around 35.4 feet that night. The river then receded back below flood stage the afternoon of the 17th. Impacts include flooding of several roads along the Guyandotte between West Hamlin and Ranger. Flooded roads include Payton Branch Road, Nine Mile Creek Road, Four Mile Creek Road, Hamilton Creek Road, Esquire Drive, and Health Creek Road.

The Tug Fork Fork River at Litwar exceeded its flood stage of 24 feet the night of February 15, then rose to a crest near 31 feet overnight. The river returned below flood stage the morning of the 16th. Major flooding impacted homes along the river between Iaeger and Panther, County Route 1, and several secondary roads.

The Guyandotte River at Logan exceeded its flood stage of 23 feet the night of February 15, then rose to a crest around 28.1 feet overnight. The river returned below flood stage the morning of the 16th. Impacts include flooding of the power plant, and roads and railroad tracks near the town.

The Guyandotte River at Pineville exceeded its flood stage of 13 feet the night of February 15, then rose to a crest around 14.1 feet overnight. The river returned below flood stage the next morning. Impacts include flooding of some homes and businesses along Rockcastle Creek near Pine Avenue and Main Street. Flooding of some homes near the confluence of Williams Branch Creek and the Guyandotte.

The Ohio River at Point Pleasant exceeded its flood stage of 40 feet the morning of February 17, then rose to a crest around 42.6 feet overnight. Impacts include flooding of Little Kyger Road and Blaville Road in Ohio, low lying areas around Point Pleasant, the amphitheater floods halfway up the steps, Salt Creek Road, Hannan Trace Road, Huntington Road at Boggs Run Road and Mason Eighty Road.

The Ohio River at Huntington exceeded its flood stage of 50 feet the night of February 17, then rose to a crest around 51 feet the following morning. The river then eased below flood stage shortly after midnight on the 19th. Impacts include flooding of WV Route 2 at Glenwood, Route 60 East, Main Street, and above Pats Branch. Low lying sections near the river also flood.

During this time period, low sections of Twelvepole Creek Road and Frank Branch Road flooded, along with low-lying fields adjacent to the creek.

Blaine Creek near Blaine exceeded a bankfull level of 17 feet on the afternoon of April 3rd. The creek initially crested late that night, but rose to a second, higher crest around 20.3 feet the afternoon of the 4th. The creek then receded back into its banks early in the morning on the 5th. Blaine Elementary School, Blaine Community Park, a log home downstream of the gauge, low sections of County Route 201, Left and Right Fork Laurel Road, and agricultural fields adjacent to the gauge were flooded in the midst of the swollen creek.

The Mud River near Griffithsville exceeded its bankfull level of 12 feet on the morning of April 3rd, then reached a crest around 13.2 feet that afternoon. The river fell back into its banks that night, but rose back above bankfull the following morning. After a second, slightly lower crest, the river returned to, and remained within, its banks the evening of the 4th. During the times the river was out of its banks, fields and low areas along the river flooded.

The Mud River at Hamlin rose above its bankfull level of 13 feet late in the morning on April 3rd. The river rose to a crest near 14.9 feet on the evening of the 4th, then returned to its banks the next morning. Sections of Route 3 in West Hamlin, a house and ball fields near the High School Bridge, low areas near the high school marquee, Peppermint Lane and surrounding fields in Myra, and low areas along the Mud River between Palermo and Hamlin flooded in the midst of the river being out of its banks.

Twelvepole Creek near Wayne exceeded a bankfull level of 19 feet on the evening of April 3rd. The creek initially crested just above, and then fell back below, bankfull overnight. The creek rose back out of its banks the next morning, reaching a crest of around 23.6 feet on the evening of the 4th. The creek then slowly receded into its banks the morning of the 5th. Athletic fields in Shirley Burgess Park, Bridge Street, Wayne City Park, low sections of Mose Asbury Road, and Athletic fields at Twelvepole Valley park were flooded during this time period.

Symmes Creek at Aid exceeded a bankfull level of 19 feet on the morning of April 4th. The creek rose to a crest around 21.4 feet the night of the 4th. A second, lower crest occurred the evening of the 6th, then the creek receded back into its banks the morning of the 8th. Low sections of Symmes Creek Road, Route 378, Route 217, and fields adjacent to the creek flooded in the midst of the swollen creek.

Tygarts Creek above Olive Hill exceeded a bankfull level of 10 feet on the morning of April 4th. The creek rose to a crest around 10.6 feet and then receded back into its banks later that morning. While the creek was out of its banks, Bond Hollow Road and fields adjacent to the creek flooded.

Tygarts Creek near Greenup exceeded a bankfull level of 20 feet on the evening of April 4th. The creek rose to a crest around 20.1 feet and then receded back into its banks early the next morning. Low areas along Route 7 and Route 2070, and the country store in Load flooded as a result.

Twelvepole Creek at Lavalette exceeded a bankfull level of 19 feet on the morning of April 4th. The creek rose to a crest around 20.3 feet that night, then receded back into its banks the next morning. While the creek was out of its banks, low sections of Plymale Branch Road, Sugarwood Golf Course, and Creekside Golf Course flooded.

The Shade River near Chester exceeded a bankfull level of 16 feet on the morning of April 4th, After reaching a crest near 19.8 feet the next morning, the creek returned below bankfull the evening of the 5th. As a result, low sections of Scout Camp Road, the Sugar Run Creek bridge, and fields adjacent to the creek were flooded.

The Shade River near Chester rose above a bankfull level of 16 feet for a second time on the night of April 6th, crested around 16.8 feet, and then receded below bankfull the next morning. While the river was out of its banks, low sections of Scout Camp Road and fields adjacent to the creek were flooded.

Raccoon Creek at Adamsville exceeded a bankfull level of 21 feet on the morning of April 7th. After cresting near 21.2 feet that evening, the creek returned below bankfull the next afternoon. Creek View Drive and the Canoe Livery Road near the Route 588 Bridge, Museum buildings near the Route 588 bridge, Bob Evans campground, Garners Ford Road, and low areas near Raccoon Creek flooded while out of its banks.

The Mud River above Milton exceeded a bankfull level of 19 feet on the morning of April 4th. After reaching a crest near 22.4 feet early the next morning, the creek returned below bankfull on the afternoon of the 5th. Low spots along Girl Scout Camp, East and West Mud River Road had flooded during the time the river was out of its banks.

Duck Creek at Macksburg exceeded a bankfull level of 13 feet on the evening of April 3rd. After cresting around 14.6 feet the night of the 4th, the creek returned to its banks the morning of the 5th. Waters briefly rose back above bankfull during the afternoon and evening of the 6th. The campground next to the gage, Broad Street, Main Street, and fields next to the creek flooded as a result. State Route 821 was also closed due to flooding between Main Street and Crooked Tree Road.

The Little Muskingum River at Bloomfield exceeded a bankfull level of 16 feet on the morning of April 4th. After cresting around 23.9 feet during the afternoon, the river returned to its banks the morning of the 5th. Bloomfield Church Road near the gage, Route 26 near Route 260, and fields between the river and Route 26 were flooded amid the river being out of its banks.

Duck Creek below Whipple exceeded a bankfull level of 12 feet on the morning of April 4th. After cresting around 15.8 feet that afternoon, the river returned to its banks the morning of the 5th. Middle Island Creek at Little exceeded a bankfull level of 14 feet on the morning of April 4th. The Little Sandy River at Grayson exceeded its flood stage of 21 feet on the morning of April 4th, then continued to rise to a crest around 23.8 feet that night. The river slowly receded and eventually fell back below flood stage the afternoon of the 5th. While the river was out of its banks, low areas, farmland, camps, and a few homes adjacent to the river were flooded.

The Muskingum River at Beverly rose above a flood stage for a second time on the morning of April 6th. The river crested around 29.4 feet that afternoon, then fell back below flood stage in the evening. Low areas, farmland, camps, and a few homes were flooded during that timeframe.

An EF1 tornado began between US 19 and Whispering Pines Lanes in the Pine Grove community of Fayette County. The tornado skipped along in an east-southeasterly direction with the damage path ending near the intersection of Mountain Vista Drive and US 60 in the Lookout community. Tree damage was extensive along Edmond Road and between Lansing Edmond Road and US 60 with the trunks of some healthy mature hardwood trees snapped in both locations and many trees uprooted. A tornado touchdown was along Kimberly Road, about 4 miles from Nelsonville. The tornado reached maximum intensity along Matheny Road to State Route 691. Matheny Road is also called York Township Road 269.  Damage was concentrated along Matheny Road and State Route 691.  The low level circulation was evident in the damage along Matheny Road.  Debris was strewn one way on the south side of the road, then in the opposite direction on the north side.  One resident said, you could see stuff flying through the air.  Then the noise got real loud and we ran into the house and into a closet.  The house was just shaking.   Several mobile homes were completely destroyed. Yet, some of these mobile homes were poorly anchored or not anchored at all. Many large softwood trees were uprooted or snapped at their trunks.  Reports were received of several cows being lifted by the tornado.  A hay bale weighing 1800 pounds was lofted into the air and set back down.  The maximum wind gusts were estimated at 120 to 130 mph.  A total of 7 people were injured.   About 13 homes were destroyed, with dozens of other homes damaged.||Since 1950, this is only the second confirmed tornado in Athens County.  The previous tornado was a F1 during May of 1980.  However, prior to 1950, 3 tornadoes have been reported in Athens County, back in July of 1896, April of 1922, and June of 1937.  The June 1937 tornado killed 3.   The storm in 1896 was reported in Glouster. However, historical accounts also describe a tornado in the late 1800s that destroyed a large grove of sycamore trees in the city of Athens.

The upstream tornado lifted, as the rear flank downdraft of the rotating thunderstorm took over.  This downburst became the dominant feature in The Plains and around the community of Athens.  The width of the damage path widened to about a quarter of a mile.  Winds were estimated as high as 100 mph in The Plains.  As the storm approached, soccer players, fans, coaches, and referees took shelter in the locker rooms, the wrestling rooms, and the lounge for teachers at Athens County High School.  About a dozen adults took shelter in the concession stand.  A few of these parents were injured when the roof was heavily damaged.  The light poles, the press box, and the scoreboard were also damaged or destroyed.  On the roof of the high school, large air condition units were blown off and damaged parked cars.  Several homes were destroyed or damaged.  Roof damage was widespread.  As the wind reached the eastern sections of the town of Athens, the maximum wind gusts were estimated at 80 to 100 mph.  The last significant damage was to an automobile service and towing garage.  The total distance of this downburst was on the order of 10 miles.  A total of 6 people were injured.  About 17 homes were destroyed, many others were damaged.||Including both this downburst and the tornado, Ohio Emergency Managment Agency categorized around 30 homes as destroyed, 51 homes with major damage, and 83 homes with minor damage.

This tornado originiated in Fairfield County, but got stronger in western Perry County.  The damage path widened as it crossed several north to south oriented roads.  A convergent damage pattern was evident.  Large trees were snapped along Avalon Road.  A greater swath of tree and structural damage was along Otterbein Road.  The damage path widened to as much as 800 yards, though the southern portion of the path was dominant.  The tornado unleashed it worst winds as it continued east to encounter Palomino Road and County Township Road 138.  At this stage, there was aproximately a 1 mile long and 100 yard wide path of EF2 strength winds, estimated at 110 to 120 mph.  A manufactured home on Palomino Road was missing 95 percent of it roof covering and 40 to 50 percent of the roof supports and interior ceilings were missing.  The woman inside was injured when a hallway door struck her in the back.  There were at least 2 eyewitnesses to the actual tornado.  Almost a mile east on County Township Road 138 a cluster of houses was heavily damaged.  The worst damage was a newer 2 story single family home, but seemed to be of the manufactured home quality.  Its roof and garage were completely blown off and thrown away.   The tornado began to weaken as it headed across County Road 25.  The tornado further weakened during its final 1.5 miles, ending near the intersection of County Roads 122, 123, and 134.   About 8 homes were destroyed in this tornado.

The western Perry County tornado lifted, but its associated rotating thunderstorm continued moving over the central portion of the county.  A new tornado touchdown occurred near Melon Hill Road about 3 miles east of New Lexington.  This tornado reached its peak intensity as it crossed near the curved portion of Route 92, about 3 miles south of Crooksville.  The EF1 damage was about 300 yards wide and roughly a mile long, including roofs and portions of roofs blown off several structures.  Peak winds in this vicinity were estimated at 100 to 110 mph.   This tornado continued for a slight distance into northwestern Morgan County.  The tornado was weakening as it crossed the county line.||The total damage from the 2 tornadoes in Perry County included 12 homes with minor damage, 16 homes with major damage, and 8 homes destroyed.

The tornado that touch downed in eastern Perry County continued into western Morgan County, before dissipating.  There were several downed trees and large branches along McKinley Street.  Three houses had minor damage and one vehicle was destroyed.  Electricity was out for over 24 hours.||Since 1950, this is the first confirmed tornado in Morgan County.  However, prior to 1950, one tornado was reported in Morgan County back in June of 1928.

A new rotating supercell formed south of thunderstorm complex that caused the tornado and strong downburst in western Athens County.  A new tornado formed. Significant structural damage to farm buildings and a few homes occurred along Eden Ridge Road.  This road is also County Route 50.  The tornado path then went across State Route 124 between community of Reedsville and Eden along the Ohio River.  A majority of the mobile homes affected were in this vicinity.  In addition, a well built single family home and its detached commercial grade garage were completely destroyed.  The foundations of both structures were wiped clean.  The EF3 damage included this area along State Route 124.  Maximum wind gusts of 150 mph were estimated.  The county reported 22 structures destroyed or having major damage, including mostly mobile and single family homes.  However, one car repair shop was also included.  Another 20 homes were affected or had minor damage.  Around a dozen outbuildings were damaged or destroyed.   One male received rib and leg fractures when his truck was flipped over while he was in it.  A woman was injured when she was pinned in rubble from her mobile home.  In the dark, her barking dog helped first responders find her faster.  A total of 6 people were injured, 2 seriously.         ||This tornado crossed the Ohio River and killed a man immediately on the other side of the river in southern Wood County of West Virginia.

This tornado originated in northeastern Meigs County Ohio and crossed the Ohio River, just upstream of the lock and dam and the community of Belleville.  A small pocket of EF3 damage located along Route 68 in the valley and flood plain along the river.  The maximum wind gusts were estimated at 160 mph here.  Also, the width of the tornado briefly widened to 500 yards here.  Well built single family homes received major damage or were destroyed.  In this area, a 57 year old male was killed.  He, his wife, and their dog had gone downstairs into the basement for protection.  The husband went back upstair to get a flashlight.  He figured the electricity would go out, as darkness had already set in.  At that point, he disappeared as the tornado hit.  His wife tried to open the door to let him back down, but she could not open the door. Their ranch style home with a brick front was destroyed.  His body was found some 150 to 200 feet away in a field.  Ten other people were injured, but none seriously.  Other significant structural and tree damage occurred along a river access road and basically along the South Fork of Lee Creek drainage toward Rockport.  The total path length of this tornado from Meigs County Ohio into Wood County was over 9 miles.   All total, the county reported 10 homes destroyed, 6 homes with major damage, and 27 homes with minor damage.  About 15 to 18 outbuildings were damaged or destroyed.

The tornado crossed the Tug Fork River from Lawrence County, Kentucky and enter Wayne County.  Numerous trees were blown down near Glenhayes. The tornado passed between Dunlow and Radnor, then into the Kiahsville and Cove Gap vicinity along Route 37.  In the Dunlow vicinity, the damage was from hilltop to hilltop, just over a half mile wide.  In that vicinity, about 5 homes were destroyed with 1 sustaining major damage.  At least 3 vehicles were damaged in Dunlow. The East Lynn Lake campground vicinity saw toppled trees and damage to electric and phone lines.  Approximately 15 homes were destroyed with 7 sustaining major damage around Kiahsville and Cove Gap.  The homes included mobile homes and manufactured structures.  A 2 story house lost its roof, plus several of the outside walls and an interior wall.  The hillsides and narrow roads were littered with uprooted trees, tangled power lines, sheets of metal roofing, and damaged vehicles. A resident near Cove Gap said, we never thought anything like this would get in here.  It got in and it didn't want to leave. I guess it wasn't here that long, but it seemed like forever.   ||Ironically, it may have been a local funeral that saved lives.  A funeral was being held in the community of Wayne that evening for a local Cove Gap resident.  Several neighbors attended the funeral and were not at home when the storm hit.  When they returned, they found their homes damaged.  The tornado then traveled into Lincoln County where it weakened and finally dissipated.||A maximum wind speed of 138 mph was estimated by the survey team in the Dunlow vicinity, resulting in a low end EF3 rating.

The long tracked tornado was weakening as it finally dissipated in Lincoln County.  Wind gusts were estimated in the 85 to 90 mph range in tree damage around Ranger.  On the enhanced Fujita scale it would be on the low end of the 1 rating.

A separate supercell that was further north and slightly later in time produced a second tornado in Lincoln County.  Damage to trees and a few residents were noted around Palermo and also along Sulphur Spring Road near Alkol.  Similar to the other tornado in Lincoln County, maximum winds were estimated on the low end of the EF1 scale, in the 85 to 90 mph range.

Rain estimated at 2 to 2.5 inches in less than 3 hours fell over a small area north of Sherman. There was a mud slide where Skull Run crosses Route 68.  The debris had to be pushed off the road.

Downpours were oriented northwest to southeast across Gallia County with the heaviest rain south of the Route 35 corridor. This included the Centenary area.  Rains of 2.5 to 4 inches occurred between 1130E and 1330E.  One automatic gauge near Northup measured 4.02 inches of rain in about 2 hours and 20 minutes.  A gauge in Rio Grande measured 2.6 inches of rain.||Flash flooding occurred, centered on the Chickamauga Creek basin, including its Little Chichamauga tributary. Raccoon Creek also received much of the runoff from these downpours. Clear Fork, a small tributary to Raccoon Creek, flooded along the Router 141 corridor.  This caused students from both Green Elementary School and Gallia Academy High School to be held after hours until the water receded from their access road.  Urban runoff from paved surfaces quickly got inside convenience stores.  Buildings in the 4H fairgrounds were flooded.  The fast flowing water washed away small culverts, damaged roads, and private driveways.  Basements were flooded.  Vehicles were damaged by flood waters. One local farmer said he lived there his entire life and has never seen flooding like this.  A woman at the University of Rio Grande said she had never seen anything like it, and it was horrible. ||Portions of several state routes were closed by flood waters, including Jackson Pike around the Holzer Medical Center and the 4H fairgrounds.  Also along the Jackson Pike, water surrounded, but did not get inside about 30 mobile homes in the Park Lane trailer court.  As the water was receding, state maintenance trucks used their snow plows to help push mud and debris off area roads.||Thankfully, there were no injuries according to Gallia County Sheriff Joe Browning.  The Gallia County Emergency Management said besides the one business, there were 25 to 30 homes impacted, but no one contacted them for assistance.
The headwaters of Grassy Run flooded Route 47 and the Tanner Road near the Gilmer County line.  Rain was estimated at 1 to 2 inches in less than 3 hours.
Minor flash flooding occurred.  Small streams such as Arnold Creek near Central Station flooded roads.  Rain was estimated at 1 to 1.5 inches in less than 3 hours.

Rain maximums of 2 to 3 inches fell in central Lawrence County in 3 to 6 hours.  Several small streams flooded and closed roads.  Some of the highest water was along McKinney Creek and County Route 36. The water surrounded a few homes.  Water got inside a garage.  Water from the headwaters of Ice Creek also flooded County Route 6 around Rock Camp.

Small private bridges to homes were washed out.  Roads were damaged.  A few homes had minor basement flooding.||The axis of this small heavy rain area crossed the state border.  Flash flooding also occurred in a small section of McDowell County, West Virginia.

Estimated rain amounts of 2 to 3.5 inches in less than 3 hours over a small portion of the county along the Virginia border.  A gauge south of the heavy axis at Jackson Flats measured around 2.2 inches.||Flash flooding occurred along the deep narrow valleys comprising both forks of Bull Creek.  At the headwaters of the Left Fork of Bull Creek, the Mud Fork and the Road Fork also flooded.  The feeder streams into Panther Creek called Greenbrier Fork and Trap Fork also flooded.  The terrain varies about 800 feet between the ridge tops and hollows.  One sleeping resident was warned by a phone call.  A neighbor told her, your car is floating in your driveway.  Another resident said, I've been here 25 years, and this is about the worst we've ever had.    ||Preliminary damage assessment had 1 house destroyed. Two other houses had minor damage and 49 others were affected. Two restaurants had minor damage. Fifty small private bridges and 20 vehicles were damaged.  Personnel from the West Virginia National Guard were used to gain access to remote areas.  The adjacent roads to these streams had sections washed out or undermined.||Localized flash flooding also occurred across the state border in Buchanan County, Virginia.

She had minor injuries.  It was observed that most of the old large trees that fell in the park had extensive rot within their trunks. ||Around a dozen homes had some degree of damage, mostly to their roofs. A tornado occurred along the Left Fork of French Creek and County Route 20 in eastern Pleasants County.  The rating was based on the damage to healthy hardwood trees, with peak wind gusts near 100 mph.  Many trees were snapped or uprooted.  One small metal outbuilding was destroyed. The EF1 tornado along the Left Fork of French Creek in Pleasants County crossed Old State Road and continued into northern Ritchie County.  The maximum gusts were near 100 mph in Ritchie County too. The path ended near Route 16.  The total path length in both counties was just over 4 miles.||A single family house had damage to windows and roofing.  Large trees were snapped.  Thankfully, there were no fatalities or injuries.

The tornado touched down on a ridge along Chapman Lane.  This is off of County Route 48 southeast of Lost Creek.  Numerous trees were downed.  The tornado continued across County Route 52 where additional trees and power lines were blown down.  At this point, the tornado struck the Johnstown United Methodist Church.  The church was of brick construction, originally from 1884.  Modifications have been made to the structure over the years.  It is believed the roof was lifted from the church and then fell back into place.  In doing so, it caused structural damage to the back brick wall.  The church steeple was also damaged.  Even some tombstones in the cemetery were blown over and damaged by fallen debris. Several large trees were blown down around the church.  Some of those trees were over 100 years old. The tornado lifted near the next ridge.||The strongest wind gusts were estimated near 100 mph based on the healthy trees that were snapped and uprooted, plus the structural damage to the church.

A recreational vehicle was flipped over and destroyed in the Century No. 2 vicinity.  Trees were snapped.  An auto shop was damaged.  Its back wall was blown out. Sections of an old metal roof were peeled off.  Two cars has minor damage from fallen debris.

Rains estimated at 1 to 2 inches fell in less than 2 hours.  Minor flash flooding occurred along small creeks west of the Interstate 79 corridor.  Water flowed over roads.  One example was northeast of Camden, where the Dry Fork flooded near the intersection with Rush Run Road.  No structures were flooded.

Minor flash flooding occurred when small streams at the headwaters of the Guyandotte River, plus the Piney Creek basin, flooded roads. Near Besoco, the water was a few feet deep over the roads. Highway crews cleared debris off the roads.  No structures were known to have flooded.
The headwaters of Elkhorn Creek flooded roads around Maybeury and Switchback.  Roads such as Powerhouse Hill, Route 52/38, and Route 901/56 were closed.  Roads were undermined in a few spots.
Small streams along Route 210, such as Lick Creek, flooded roads.   In the Nats Creek vicinity near the Martin County line, roads were flooded.  No homes were flooded.

Both urban and rural flash flooding occurred during the early evening hours of a Friday night.  Numerous streets in Ashland were flooded with several vehicles flooded.  Water even pooled on their high school football field from the overwhelmed drainage system, causing the first game of the season to be canceled.   ||Vehicles were also flooded on roads around Summit and Ironville. In Ironville, some people were trapped in houses surrounded by water.  In the Cannonsburg vicinity, streams along Route 3 such as Laurel Creek and Lower Chadwick Creek flooded.   One house had its first floor flooded, and its residents were rescued from the second floor.
Areas near the Mingo County line, such as Cow Creek and the headwaters of Island Creek flooded and closed roads.

The hardest hit area by flash flooding was around Myrtle.  Duncan Fork was 3 feet above bankfull as it flowed into Trace Fork.  Nearby Riffle Branch also flooded the road.  The roads were closed.  Water was reported around one house in the Lenore vicinity of Laurel Fork.  ||A mobile home in the Delbarton vicinity was moved off of its foundation by water and debris flowing off a saturated mountainside.||Around a dozen homes around the county had water inside. About 32 residents had water around their homes.  Basement flooding was common. Several private wells were contaminated. Local volunteer fire department personnel helped residents that had their homes surrounded by high water.

Streams such as Whites Creek, Walker Branch, and Dock Creek flooded in the northern portion of the county.  Small sections of roads were damaged.  A rock and debris slide blocked both lanes of Route 52.   Minor stream flooding also occurred in the southern portion of the county around Dunlow.

Urban and rural flash flooding occurred.  Many streets in Huntington were flooded including the usual viaducts.  The water caused some road damage.  Water was 1 to 2 feet deep in spots.  Water seeped into businesses, the Marshall University library, and the basement of a hospital. A discount store on 5th Avenue lost some merchandise. An animal hospital off of Route 60 was flooded, but the dogs and cats inside were saved. On 25th Street, water was into some homes.  Several vehicles were flooded when trapped in the high water.    ||Outside of the city, small streams such as Fourpole and Grapevine Branch flooded roads.

Culverts were washed out on Messinger Way off of Swamp Run Road near Audra State Park.  Residents in about 8 homes could not get out.  A culvert on Hardman Road, or County Route 3/9, was also washed out.

The building housing the Lincoln County 911 Center took a lightning hit.  Personnel think the lightning hit their radio tower then ran across the roof of the building. A dispatcher described the sound as marbles being dropped on the metal roof.||The phone system and some radio equipment were damaged.  Calls to the center were transferred to Boone County for about 3 hours.
Lightning struck an office building off of Teays Valley Road and ignited a fire.  The fire was in the attic. The building sustained smoke and water damaged.

Small streams, such as Mud Fork, Trap Fork and Greenbrier Creek, flooded roads and surrounded a few homes in the western portion of the county.   No homes were flooded.

Poor drainage flooding was common along streets during the late afternoon into the early evening.  One low spot collected water about a foot deep on New Goff Mountain Road near Cross Lanes. Small streams and headwater rivers flooded roads.  One example, the upper Gauley River was flooding sections of Route 42.

The West Fork of Twelvepole Creek and other streams were flooding during the morning of the 4th.  Eventually, flooding became restricted to near the major rivers, including the Ohio.  Roads were blocked by the high water.

Minor small stream flooding occurred during the afternoon into the evening of the 4th.  Back water flooding from the swollen Kanawha River continued through much of the 5th.  The main result was road blockages.
Small streams flooding begin by early afternoon on the 4th.  Thirteenmile Creek and Popular Fork flooded roads.  Minor flooding continued along the Kanawha and Ohio River into the 6th.

Small stream flooding began in scattered locations about the county by early afternoon on the 4th.  One example was Lower Creek flooding roads near Milton. Creeks overflowed and blocked roads.  A few examples, included Georges Creek and Nats Creek.
Small streams, mostly in the southern part of the county, flooded roads during the evening hours on the 10th.

Minor small stream flooding occurred during the evening hours on the 10th.  The Little Sandy River crested at 21.6 feet around 0200E on the 11th at Grayson.  Flood stage is 21 feet. A few roads remained blocked until near dawn.

Duck Creek and the Little Muskingum River had minor overflow and blocked roads during the day on the 11th.

Numerous roads were closed due to overflowing streams.  One example was Indian Creek Road near Huttonsville. A strong rise on the Middle Fork and upper Tygart Valley River flooded fields and caused several roads to remain closed into the afternoon hours. Small streams overflowed and blocked roads in scattered locations about the county.  One example was Little Laurel Run flooding Union Road south of Philippi.  ||The Tygart Valley River exceeded flood stage at Belington on the 11th, during the afternoon. The crest at Belington was 15.9 feet during the predawn hours of the 12th.  This caused a few road closures to linger into the 12th.  However, water levels were over a foot less, compared to the flood of the previous week.

Several small streams caused minor flooding of roads.  One example was Shinns Run near Shinnston.  The strong rise on the West Fork also caused some minor water problems, but the river crested under stage.

Along the county border the Middle Fork River caused minor flooding. Boy Scout Camp Road was flooded.  ||A strong rise on the Buckhannon River caused minor overflow, but levels remained just below flood stage.

A huge land slide, off a man made hill side off of Yeager Airport, blocked the normal flow of Elk Two Mile in the hollow below.  The resultant flooding surrounded about 20 homes, and damaged 9 of these dwellings.  At least one vehicle was flooded.  The damage from the land slide was even more extensive.

A man-made extension to a steep hill side was constructed and finished back in 2007.  It was located at the end of the main runway at Yeager Airport.  The large land fill allowed space for an engineered material arresting system for airplane safety. ||A huge section of that steep hill side came sliding down just after 11000E on the 12th.  Through the night and into the early morning hours of the 13th, the slide continued to fan out in the hollow below.  A church and 2 houses were destroyed by the slide.  Power lines and poles were also destroyed.

Streams overflowed with minor flooding.  Symmes Creek overflowed and blocked roads, such as Route 378 and 217 near Willow Wood.  Minor flooding also occurred along the Ohio River into the 16th, but the crest was lower than on the 6th and 7th of the month.

The Ohio River rose higher along its shore with Greenup County than the crest on the 7th of March.  Minor flooding of parks occurred. Back water flooding also was seen up feeder streams.  The broad crest was around 54.7 feet at Greenup Lock and Dam during the evening hours of the 14th.  Flood stage is 54 feet.
The crest on the Greenbrier river was just under 11 feet at Marlinton, about 1 foot above bank full.  Minor flooding of roads occurred.

The Ohio River crested above flood stage again during the evening of the 14th.  The level at Ashland was around 53.6 feet.  Flood stage is 53 feet.  This crest was 1 to 2 feet lower than the recent high water on the 6th and 7th of the month.  A few flood gates were installed in the flood walls including the town of Catlettsburg.  Low lying areas and up feeder streams saw minor flooding.
A barn on Harris Road sustained minor damage after being struck by lightning.  Damage was limited to the electrical panel and about 3 to 4 feet of the adjacent wall.

Numerous roads were blocked by flooding small streams throughout the county.  Several culverts were damaged or washed out, damaging and closing roads. Blaine and Webbville Fire Departments, plus Cherryville Fire and Rescue, responded to individuals in stalled flooded vehicles.  A few examples of flooding included Buck Branch, which was blocking 3 D Road and getting around a few houses.  Flooding occurred along Georges Creek around Charley. ||Total 24 hour rain amounts reached 2.5 to 4 inches during this flooding.||The county damage assessment was 6 homes destroyed and 8 others with major damage.  Another dozen homes and 2 businesses had minor damage.  About 8 homes were classified as in a major risk due to hillside slides.  Around 43 small private bridges or culverts were destroyed.

Numerous streams overflowed and blocked roads.   Examples were Newcomb Creek and Lynn Creek near East Lynn, Lick and Cove Creeks near Kiahsville, plus Mill Creek near Saltpetre.  Some homes near Kiahsville were impacted. A few homes along Mill Creek were flooded.  Small private bridges were washed out.  Road culverts were damaged.  A couple of vehicles were found in Mill Creek. ||A 62 year old woman tried to walk out of Rowe Hollow in the Amilda vicinity.  She was going to attend a Good Friday evening service at the neighborhood church around 1800E on the 3rd. The unnamed run, that flows out of the hollow and into the East Fork of Twelvepole Creek, was flowing across the dead end gravel road.  Its assigned route number is 701/38. The water was about knee deep. Neighbors were shocked to see her try to walk through the water with her umbrella. She fell down. The water in the road washed her down the road. She could not straighten up. She was swept away and drowned. Her body was found in the East Fork of Twelvepole Creek.||A rain gauge along Mill Creek measured 2.25 inches in 3 hours during the early evening with a 24 hour total of 3.6 inches.

The headwaters of the Mud River also flooded.||Small private bridges to local residents were damaged or destroyed.  One of those bridges was located along Bulger Road.

In the southwestern part of the county, West Brinegar Road had a culvert wash out from Macabee Creek.||The Little Sandy River crested nearly 3 feet higher, compared to the high water on the 11th of March. Some barns and outbuildings were also surrounded by water.

After the flash flooding, the larger creeks and the Big Coal River overflowed and blocked roads into the morning of the 4th.  The crest on the Big Coal River at Ashford was around 20.6 feet, or about 3 feet lower than the 5th of March.

The larger creeks flooded in the wake of the heaviest rain.  Blaine Creek rose about 15 feet in the vertical and crested around 19 feet between midnight and dawn on the 4th.  Roads, including Route 32, were flooded.

An automatic rain gauge measured 2.35 inches of rain in less than 2 hours.  Initially, the ground was relatively dry. Yet, minor flash flooding occurred along a few small streams and runs in the steep terrain. For example, Upper Glade Run overflowed into buildings at Camp Caesar, a 4-H facility.

Rain amounts of 1.5 to 2 inches fell in less than 2 hours.  Runoff flowed across roads in the vicinity of Craigsville and Richwood from overflowing ditch lines and from adjacent steep mountain slopes.  Ponding of water on the streets in poor drainage areas was common. No road closures were reported.
A large section of metal roofing was blown off a shell building along Route 2565, just south of Louisa.
A gauge south of Louisa measured 2.3 inches of rain in less than 2 hours.  Fields flooded along Two Mile Creek.
Trees were blown down.  Sheds and 1 home had roof damage.

The maximum wind speed was estimated at 107 mph by a National Weather Survey team.  The damage swath consisted mostly of hardwood trees that were downed and snapped along Country Club Road approximately 3 miles northeast of Richwood. There were also wooden utility poles that were snapped, along with some shingle damage to 1 home.   The tornado and tree damage continued into Greenbrier County just south of Summit Lake.
Four large trees were uprooted along Route 119.  This caused damaged to a metal yard fence.

The tornado began near the intersection of Old Route 38 and Route 38, just east of the Sugar Creek Bridge.  Several trees were snapped at the trunk and uprooted along the damage path.  One home sustained significant siding damage.  The siding was torn off the west side of the house and thrown about 100 feet into a field to the north.  A few flatbed single axle trailers were flipped in the front yard of another residence.  Eight utility poles were down by falling trees and wind.  Near the end of the path, a 4 inch diameter branch penetrated the roof of a home.  The end of the damage path was along Route 38, about a quarter mile past Reger Road.
Small creeks in the far northern portion of the county flooded.  A few examples included Barren Creek. It flood a road and a garage.  Goose Creek spilled over roads near the Pocatalico River.
Streams overflowed over roads.  Camp Creek had 1 foot of water, with some pavement damage.
Stremas overflowed onto roads.  One example was Ten Mile Creek flooding its adjacent road.

The headwaters of the Left Fork of Mud River flooded.  This included Dogbone Branch, Bear Branch, and Flat Creek.   Along Bulgar Road, the Mud River Fire Department had 2 to 3 feet of water inside.  One of their vehicles was washed into the creek.  Damage assessment included 2 homes destroyed, while 14 other homes had severe or major damage.  Several of these homes were mobile homes. Two churches also had flood damage.  Bridges and culverts were damaged. ||Further south, streams overflowed onto roads in the Harts vicinity.
Streams in the western portion of the county flooded roads.   Near the mouth of Mill Fork with Crawley Creek, 1 business flooded.  One vehicle was flooded too.
Large heavy stage props for an outdoor amphitheater were blown around at Grandview. A few pine trees were uprooted in the vicinity.
Tree branches were blown down on North Franklin Street.  They fell onto phone and power lines.

Many trees were snapped and uprooted.  Four wooden electrical transmission line poles were snapped. Several small yard items were blown around, including a dog kennel and a kayak. All the damage and debris exhibited a slightly divergent pattern, consistent with a microburst.

A single wide trailer was lifted off the ground and rolled upside down before settling on its side.  Two residents were inside the structure at the time of the tornado.  Minor injuries were sustained.  Additional tree damage was observed in the vicinity of the trailer. Structural damage to the Walmart and the Brown Food Service warehouse occurred.  Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted. Widespread flash flooding occurred on small headwater rivers, like the Cherry, plus the small streams and runs throughout the county.  Due to the saturated mountain slopes, water cascaded down mountainsides where no stream existed, as was the case in Richwood. Many water rescues took place and much of the town of Richwood was evacuated. The evacuation included a nursing home with 97 patients.  One resident of Richwood said, just seems like there was a cloudburst right back on this mountain. It just all came at one time. It was just like a big river coming down through here.  In the wake of this flooding, previously abandoned homes on the mountainside were demolished.  Severe flooding also occurred in the community of Birch River.||Peters Creek in Lockwood crested near 17 feet around 1845E after rising over 11 feet in the vertical. ||The flash flooding transitioned into river flooding along the Gauley, upstream of Summersville Dam, and along the Meadow River and the border with Fayette County.
The severe flash flooding transitioned into river flooding on the Gauley and Meadow Rivers.

Severe flash flooding occurred in scattered locations throughout the county.  Runoff also cascaded down steep mountains, generating their own water channels. ||Stream flooding transitioned into severe river flooding on the upper Gauley River during the evening of the 23rd.  ||The combination of both the flash flooding and river flooding destroyed on the order of 60 to 70 homes.  About 15 to 20 dwellings sustained major damage, with another 15 to 20 houses having minor flood damage.

The flash flooding along the streams transitioned into river flooding along the Gauley and upper Elk Rivers. ||The highest stage on record occurred on the Gauley River at Camden on Gauley.  See the episode narrative for the specifics. Of the 30 homes along Riverside Drive in Camden on Gauley, only 8 were located high enough on the hill to avoid the flood waters.

The flood of record occurred on the lower Elk River around Clendenin.  ||Two women died. They were trying to save family heirlooms in the basement of a home in Elkview.  In likely their last cell phone contact, 1 of the 2 women described the scene, as like the Titanic. An elderly man also died in his home in Elkview.  Another young woman died, but the situation was unknown. | |Both the flash flooding and the river flooding were severe, but the amount of damage from the record river flooding was likely higher in Kanawha County, than the damage from the flash flooding.

Flash flooding occurred in scattered locations, mostly in the northern half of the county.  In Ravenswood, a small stream along Utah Road called Lick Run is usually ankle deep. It rose 6 feet. A 4 year old toddler slipped into the water. The grandfather jumped in, but could not rescue him. His body was found the following day, about a quarter mile away. ||A preliminary damage assessment was done in this county.  It had 10 homes destroyed and about 2 dozen with damage.

Severe flash flooding occurred in scattered locations along several streams.  One stream was Porter Creek in the Bomont area. One 9 year resident in Bomont said, I really do not imagine how this would happen. It's just heartbreaking to see all the homes floating down the creek.  A few of the other streams included Laurel Creek near Paxton and Big Otter near Ivydale.||This initial flash flooding along the small streams transitioned into river flooding along the Elk River.

Flash flooding transitioned into river flooding along the Elk River during the late afternoon and early evening.  The river flooding continued into the morning of the 24th.||Damage associated with the river flooding may have exceeded that associated with the earlier flash flooding.  The Clay County 911 Center had about 2 feet of water inside. Sections of Route 4 around Procious were washed out.

Severe flash flooding occurred in the northern portion of the county during the afternoon.  A few of the streams included Smithers Creek, Brackens Creek,  Laurel Creek, and Glade Creek.||The flash flooding on the small streams transitioned into river flooding along the Meadow and lower Gauley Rivers.

River flooding occurred on the Meadow and lower Gauley Rivers along the northern border of Fayette County.  Russellville was flooded and Route 41 damaged.  One resident of Russellville said, and when it got too so much, I grabbed the kids and I left.  You couldn't stay. You'd have drowned.||A preliminary damage assessment was done in Fayette County.  In both the flash flooding and river flooding, about 15 homes were destroyed. Another dozen or so homes were damaged.

A West Virginia DOH worker was killed during the cleanup of one tree down on Union Campground Road. The worker was removing the tree from the road when it rolled over onto him.

Damage consistent with an EF-1 tornado and estimated maximum wind speeds of 110 mph was found by a National Weather Service storm survey. Many trees were snapped or uprooted along the path of the tornado. Near the start of the path along Shaws Run Road, a cinder block garage partially collapsed. The structure was under construction and the trusses had not even been installed yet, so it was just 4 walls with an open top. The house on the same property had some minor roof damage. Across the street, an old wood barn suffered a full collapse and the eastern wall blew out on two-story single family house. About a mile and a half farther along the path, along Gawthorp Lane, a house received significant roof damage, with about 20 percent of the roof decking and shingles removed, a small shed was also destroyed. Just down the block from here, a resident recalls that she had just arrived home when she heard a rush of wind. Her front window blew in as she ran for shelter deeper in the house. She remembers it being over in an instant and when she came back into the front room she could see her SUV flipped on its top in the neighbors yard, across the street from where she had parked it just minutes before. The tornado continued along just south of Sun Valley Road, with a lot of tree and power line damage along Old Davisson Run Road. Toward the end of the tornado path, damage was much lighter with just small trees and branches down near the intersection of Sun Valley Road and US 50.

A single wide mobile home, just off Ridenour Road, was shifted 3 to 4 feet off its foundation. Another trailer had roof damage and debris blown through the windows on the west facing side, and another outbuilding further east along the path had the roof ripped off. Flash flooding led to several roads being closed overnight in the Harman area, causing infrastructure damage throughout the town. The local water and sewage plant were significantly impacted and knocked offline. Numerous roads and culverts were washed out and several homes and trailers were pushed off their foundations. In total, 13 homes were damaged. Three of them were rendered uninhabitable. Sewer lines in Harman were also washed out. Many water rescues were conducted. Across the Monongahela National Forest, 68 miles of train track were damaged.

A tornado touched down 4 miles east northeast of Alum Creek, just inside the Kanawha County line. The tornado continued moving northeastward in the vicinity of Route 119 and eventually dissipated near the Kanawha River as it approached downtown Charleston. The tornado was not continuously on the ground, frequently touching down along its path. Many trees were snapped and/or uprooted, in addition to minor roof damage. Damage also occurred at Berry Hills Country Club. The survey team also noticed several areas of non-tornadic wind damage in close proximity to the tornado path.

A tornado touched down just north of Spring Hill Cemetery and traveled north northwest towards the eastern portion of Twilight Drive, tearing down several trees on the highest elevation peak. The tornado then traveled down the northern side of the hill and moved across an open field. Part of a roof was blown off an office building and a batch of large healthy trees were blown down in a circular motion at the end of the field. This is where the tornado is estimated to have been at its peak strength. The tornado then continued north northwest where it blew a steeple off of a church along Keystone Drive and then continued up the adjacent hill on the southern edge of the Charleston Airport, where it then dissipated.

A man drowned along a swollen Racoon Creek and a low spot along Route 325 near the village of Vinton.  Otherwise, county officials reported no flooding.  ||According to a state report, the driver drove partially into water covering the road, but then backed out. This was at night. The driver then pulled into a nearby driveway and asked the property owner if he thought he could make it through the water.  The property owner told the driver that if he could see the edge lines, he should be okay.  The driver then proceeded to drive into the water, where his pickup truck was caught by the current and swept downstream.  The driver was able to get out of his truck.  The property owner ran over to try to help, offering a long stick to the driver, telling him to swim toward it.  The driver was unable to make it.  His body was recovered a few hours later.

Numerous roads were blocked due to high water, including Greenbrier Road along the Dickenson/Buchanan County line. The river gage on Cranes Nest River near Clintwood showed it rose out of its 13 foot bankfull level in the early afternoon on the 6th, cresting near 14 feet in the evening. This led to flooding along Route 649 and local campgrounds adjacent to the river. Cranes Nest River receded back into its banks just before midnight that night.
Several creeks across the county rose out of their banks and led to blocked roadways.

Towns in the county were inundated with heavy rainfall which led to water entering into homes, particularly in Berwind and Coalwood. Significant flooding also led to road closures for portions of Yukon and Bradshaw. The river gage along the Tug Fork River in Bradshaw indicated the river rose above its 10 foot bankfull stage in the early afternoon on the 6th and crested at 13.5 feet later on that evening. During which time, homes downstream of the gage were flooded. The river receded below flood stage just before sunrise the next day. The Office of Emergency Services declared a local state of emergency on the morning of the 6th.
A period of heavy rainfall led to high water in the town of Welch.

Multiple roads were closed due to high water, including the 2300 block of Sullivan in Beaver, the 2500 block of Sweeneysburg Road in Beckley, the 1600 block of Hinton Road in Daniels, and the 1600 block of Ritter Road in Daniels. Residents of Violet Lane in the town of Beaver were evacuated due to water rising and blocking access along the roadway. A private driveway to a nursing home collapsed in the town of Beaver, cutting the facility off from local fire department and EMS support. A temporary access road was constructed behind the nursing home, connecting to a different road. One water rescue was performed in the east Gull/Killarney area.
High water resulted in minor flooding along Route 97 in Maben.
Two forest service campgrounds were flooded along with the park boathouse near Thurmond.

During the late night hours on the 6th, the river gage for the Tug Fork River at Williamson rose above its flood stage of 27 feet. The river crested in moderate flood, near 34 feet, on the morning of the 7th. During which time, water began to surround the water treatment plant in Williamson as well as covered Route 612 and the railroad yard in Williamson. The river returned to its banks on the evening of the 7th.
As the Ohio River began to rise in the town of Greenup, 5th Street was closed due to flooding.
Portions of State Route 3 near the town of Rush were covered in water due to the East Fork of the Little Sandy River rising out of its banks.
A portion of Yellow Creek Road collapsed due to high water near the town of Clifford.

The gage in Ashland indicated the Ohio River rose above its 52 feet minor flood stage on the afternoon of the 13th. It crested at 54.6 feet very early on the morning of the 15th, and receded back below flood stage 24 hours later on the 16th. Minor flooding of roadways in low lying areas near the river occurred during this time, mainly due to backwater.

The Ohio River rose above its 54 foot minor flood stage at the Lloyd Greenup Lock on the morning of the 14th, cresting around 55 feet just after midnight on the 15th. The river returned to its banks later on that afternoon. Minor flooding of mainly low-lying areas from backwater occurred.

Multiple roads were closed across the county due to flooding, including State Route 325, State Route 233, and State Route 141. On the evening of the 14th, a 73 year old man drowned in the flood waters at the intersection of State Route 141 and German Ridge Road. The man drove his car into the high water and was overcome by the rushing water.
Multiple roads were closed due to flooding, including State Route 329 near Broadwell, State Route 56 near Hocking, and State Route 681 near Albany.
Numerous roads were closed due to flooding, including State Route 681 in Snowville, and State Route 124 and State Route 143 in Rutland.

The intersection of State Route 93 and State Route 373 in Ironton was closed in both direction due to high water. State Route 650 was also closed due to flooding in both directions between the town of Hanging Rock and County Route 21.
State Route 233 was closed in both directions between Oak Hill and the Gallia County line due to flooding.
State Route 145 near the town of Lower Salem was closed due to high water.

The Duck Creek near Whipple rose out of its banks in the afternoon of the 13th, cresting around 12.6 feet later on that evening. The creek returned to its 12 foot bankfull level early on the morning of the 14th. Sections of State Routes 26, 821, and 145 began to flood with water on the roadways.

On the morning of February 13th, the Little Muskingum River in Bloomfield rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level. Later on that evening, the river crested just above 20 feet, and then receded back down into its banks during the early morning hours on the 14th. While the river was above its bankfull level, the intersection of Route 26 and Route 260 began to flood.

The section of the Ohio River near Ironton rose above its 52 foot minor flood stage on the morning of the 14th. It crested late that night at 52.6 feet, and returned to its banks during the early afternoon hours on the 15th. During the time the river was above its banks, low areas along Storms Creek in Ohio were flooded.

The Shade River near Chester rose out of its 17 foot bankfull level on the morning of the 13th, cresting at 18.2 feet early on the 14th. The river then returned to its banks after daybreak on the 14th. While the river was risen, minor flooding of low lying areas occurred, particularly at the Sugar Run Creek Bridge and Shade River Bridge.

The West Fork of Duck Creek near Macksburg rose above its 13 foot bankfull level on the morning of the 13th, cresting later on that afternoon at 13.81 feet. It later returned to its banks during the early morning hours on the 14th. Minor flooding occurred at the campground next to the gage, as well as a few homes on the left bank of the creek.
The Upper Mud River rose above its banks and covered the roadways of Upper Mud River Road at Big Laurel near Jenks. Upstream along the Mud River, Palermo Road also flooded near the town of Palermo.
One of two eastbound lanes were closed on US-60 near Woodland Drive due to high water.
Minor flooding on Manilla Ridge Road occurred as Eighteenmile Creek rose out of its banks.

Middle Island Creek near Middlebourne rose out of its banks on the afternoon of the 13th, and crested at 16.84 feet later on that evening. It returned below its 16 foot bankfull stage just after midnight on the 14th. Low and poor drainage areas along the creek and tributaries flooded during this time.
Ashton Upland Road became impassable during the morning hours on the 13th due to high water along the roadway.
Route 152 near Dunlow was closed due to Twelvepole Creek rising out of its banks.

The Middle Island Creek gage at Little observed the creek rising out of its 14 foot bankfull level on the evening of the 13th. It crested at 14.24 feet a few minutes after midnight and then returned to its banks just before dawn. The field opposite the gage, along with Stewarts Run Road and low areas along secondary roads near the creek, were flooded during this time period.

The Ohio River near Huntington rose out of its banks on the morning of the 14th, cresting at 50.48 feet later on that evening. It returned below its 50 foot flood stage the next morning. Many low-lying sections near the river became flooded due to backwater, West Virginia Route 2 at Glenwood being one of those areas in particular.

The Ohio River at Point Pleasant rose above its 40 foot flood stage during the late night hours on the 12th, and remained that way until the early morning hours on the 16th. This led to prolonged flooding of local roads in Point Pleasant, including Salt Creek Road, Hannan Trace Road, Huntington Road at Boggs Run Road, and Mason Eighty Road. The river crested at 43.75 feet, causing flooding to occur all the way into Ambrosia along Route 30 and 62.
Several road across the county were closed due to flooding along creeks and streams.
Betsy Branch flooded, washing out a section of Garland-Betsy Branch Road.
Multiple roads around Chattaroy and Delbarton flooded.

On the afternoon of the 20th, the Muskingum River at McConnelsville rose above its 11 foot flood stage. The river crested just below 12 feet early on the morning of the 21st, but did not return below flood stage until the morning of the 22nd. Most of the primary roads were flooded in between McConnelsville and Zanesville while the river was above flood stage, as well as a few homes that reside near the river.
Nelson Branch flooded, closing a section of Nelson Branch Road. Also, County Route 8 was closed, due to flooding along Little Huff Creek.

During the late afternoon hours on the 20th, the Muskingum River in Beverly rose above its 29 flood stage. The river crested around 31 feet early in the morning on the 21st, but did not go back below flood stage until the morning of the 22nd. Low lying areas and farmland near the river gage were flooded.

On the morning of the 19th, the Shade River near Chester rose above its 17 foot bankfull level, cresting around 17.5 feet just after midnight on the 20th, and returning to its banks later on that morning. While out of its banks, the Sugar Run Creek Bridge and Shade River Bridge were flooded, as were some low lying areas along the Shade River.

Just after sunrise on the morning of the 19th, the Little Muskingum River at Bloomfield rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level. The river crested just below 20 feet that evening, then returned to its banks in the early morning hours on the 20th. Hay fields across from the gage and areas between the river and Route 26 were flooded during this time, as well as the intersection of Route 26 and Route 260.

In the afternoon of the 19th, Duck Creek near the town of Whipple rose out of its 12 foot bankfull level, and crested at 13.26 feet that evening. The creek returned to its banks on the morning of the 20th. While out of its banks, portions of State Routes 26, 821, and 145 were flooded.

Duck Creek at Macksburg rose out of its 13 foot bankfull level on the morning of the 19th, cresting at 13.92 feet just after midnight on the 20th. It returned to its banks for a brief period of time that morning, but rose to around 13.29 feet on the evening of the 20th. The creek returned to its banks once again just before midnight on the evening of the 20th. Aside from low lying areas near the creek, a few homes on the left bank were flooded. Minor flooding also occurred along Broad Street.

The gage at Cranes Nest showed the river rose above its thirteen foot bankfull level on the morning of the 13th, returning to its banks later on that afternoon. The river crested at 13.86 feet just before noon, resulting in Route 649 and several camps along the river to flood.

Along the Little Muskingum River, the gage at Bloomfield showed the river rose above its sixteen foot bankfull stage on the afternoon of the 14th. The river rose to 17.34 feet before returning to its banks just before midnight. While above its bankfull stage, the river caused Route 26 near the intersection with Route 260 to be covered by water.

During the early afternoon on the 13th, the Dry Fork gage at Bradshaw showed the river rose above its ten foot bankfull stage. The river peaked at 11.65 feet a few hours later and then returned to its banks that evening. While in flood, the rise along the Dry Fork resulted in the beginning stages of flooding in a few houses downstream of the gage.

Multiple rounds of rain caused the West Fork of Duck Creek to oscillate over its bankfull level through the course of the night of the 8th and into the day of the 9th. The highest river level reached 13.12 feet on the evening of the 9th, finally returning to its banks for the last time a few hours later. During this time, a portion of Broad Street near the creek began to flood.

Along Knapps Creek, the gage in Huntersville showed the creek rose above its nine foot bankfull level in the late morning hours of the 30th. The creek rose to 9.59 feet before returning to its banks later on that evening. Farmland, fields and out buildings next to Knapps Creek and Browns Creek started to flood during this time.

Along the Tygart Valley River, the gage at Mill Creek showed the river rose above its eleven foot bankfull level on the afternoon of the 30th. Its highest point reached just under twelve feet later on that evening before returning to its banks after sunset. While out of its banks, County Route 39 was flooded approximately 225 feet from the bridge heading out of town.

On the West Fork of Duck Creek in Macksburg, the gage showed the creek rose above its thirteen foot bankfull level on the evening of the 13th, peaking at 13.25 feet a few hours after midnight on the 14th, then returned to its banks around daybreak. Minor flooding occurred in typical spots near the creek, such as water covering Broad Street.
A blocked culvert on Rocket Drive in Greenwood led to flooding along the roadway. Also in Greenwood, Stone Valley Road became impassable due to a debris slide.

Multiple areas along Route 74 were impassable due to high water between the towns of Pennsboro and Pullman. Near the town of Glendale, Goose Creek rose out of its banks and caused a nearby bridge to become submerged.

Generally 2 to 3.5 inches of rain fell across the upper portions of the Tygart Valley River basin. No flooding occurred, partly because local creeks and streams were running fairly low at the start of the rainfall. However, this is where the story gets interesting. The 17th was a Friday, and by mid afternoon, a dozen or more locals were swimming and hanging out on the large rocks and islands in the Middle Fork River as it meanders through Audra State Park. The water from the morning rainfall arrived into Audra State Park between 3 and 4 o'clock that afternoon. Water levels rose rapidly as the crest approached, catching those in the river by surprise. Witness accounts say the water rose 4-5 feet in under an hour, with swiftly flowing current cutting off access or even submerging some of the rock outcroppings. Three separate water rescues were performed by first responders, who rescued a total of 12 individuals.

A brief tornado touched down just south of Macksburg near the Interstate 77 corridor. This was confirmed by video evidence and an on-site survey. The damage was confined to the intersection of Highland Ridge Road and Cats Creek Road, adjacent to Interstate 77 Southbound. The tornado caused damage to a few hardwood and softwood trees. The damage consisted of some downed large softwood limbs along with a pine tree that was uprooted next to a mobile home. No structural damage was observed.

Duck Creek near Whipple rose out of its 12 foot bankfull level late in the night on February 3rd. The creek reached just above 15 feet on the afternoon of the 4th before returning to its banks just before dawn on the 5th. While the creek was out of its banks, portions of State Routes 26, 821, and 145 flooded.

On the evening of February 3rd, the Little Muskingum River near Bloomfield rose above its 16 foot bankfull level. The river crested at 23.53 feet on the afternoon of the 4th and then receded back its its banks just after midnight early on the 5th. While out of its banks, Bloomfield Church Lane near the bridge flooded.

In Grayson, the Little Sandy River rose above its 21 foot flood stage, crested at 22.04 feet later that afternoon, then returned to its banks in the evening. This resulted in high water issues along Route 773, State Route 1910, and around the Dixie Park area just past the I-64 bridge.

The Middle Fork of the Mud River near Griffithsville rose above its 12 foot bankfull level during the late morning hours on February 4th. The river returned to its banks two hours later, cresting a few inches above 12 feet before receding. This impacted fields and low lying areas both upstream and downstream of the river with a deluge of high water.

Middle Island Creek near the town of Little rose out of its 14 foot bankfull level just before midnight on February 3rd. It would not return to its banks until the late morning hours on the 5th. The river crested at 21.46 feet, which resulted in water to reach private cabins that reside near the waterway close to the Friendly Road bridge.

Middle Island Creek near Middlebourne rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level on the evening of February 3rd, crested at around 23 feet on the afternoon of the 4th, and returned to its banks during the early morning hours on the 5th. This resulted in major flooding along Route 18 and Route 24 on either side of the river. The buildings at the nearby 4H campground were also flooded, as well as the Tyler County fairgrounds.

Near the town of West Union, Middle Island Creek rose out of its 16 foot bankfull level around sunrise on the 4th. The river crested at 17.75 feet just before noon and returned to its banks shortly afterwards. Minor flooding was observed along Route 18.

The Shade River near Chester rose out of its 17 foot bankfull level late on the evening of February 3rd. The river crested at 23.33 feet and returned to its banks just before noon on the 5th. While out of its banks, the Shade River spilled onto Oak Hill Road upstream from the Shade River Bridge.

Symmes Creek in the town of Aid rose above its 19 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 4th, cresting that evening around 21.5 feet. The creek did not return to its banks until the late evening hours two days later. While out of its banks, minor flooding was observed near residential homes in close proximity to the creek.

The West Fork River in Clarksburg rose above its 14 foot flood stage for a short period of time on the evening of February 4th. The river crested at 14.01 feet and returned to its banks less than half an hour later. This resulted in nearby homes observing minor flooding and high water along Liberty Avenue.

In the town of Enterprise, the West Fork River rose out of its 17 foot bankfull level on the morning of February 4th. The river crested at 19.66 feet that evening and returned to its banks a few hours after midnight on the 5th. High water occurred during this time along roads located nearby to the gage.

On the evening of February 3rd, the West Fork of Duck Creek rose above its 13 foot bankfull level. The creek crested just below 15 feet the next morning and returned to its banks late on the evening of the 4th. This resulted in flooding along Broad Street as well as nearby homes and campgrounds.
In Spencer, Bell Street and Front Street flooded. High water was also observed along Locust Street in Reedy.

Outside of Parkersburg, Worthington Creek rose out of its banks and flooded portions of the Worthington Creek Golf Club. Near Belleville, Lee Creek Road became flooded due to the nearby creek rising out of its banks.
Walker Creek rose out of its banks on the afternoon of February 3rd and spilled onto Walker Creek Road. In the town of Mineral Wells, Pond Creek Road flooded.
Multiple streets flooded in Huntington, including 12th Street and Enslow Boulevard.

The body of an elderly man was found after being swept away by floodwaters due to Hughes River being out of its banks. The vehicle was spotted by passing motorists near State Route 47 in the Cisco area nearly submerged underwater.
Hurricane Creek rose out of its banks and spilled onto Harbour Lane in the town of Hurricane. In Winfield, flooding was observed along Tucker Branch.
Flooding was observed within the town of Mill Creek.
Deer Creek rose out of its banks and flooded onto Cass Road west of Green Bank.

Overflowing creeks led to multiple instances of flooding around the town of Wallace. High water spilled into the local hollows and resulted in minor flooding within residential homes. In the town of Enterprise, flooding on the West Fork River resulted in high water along nearby roadways. The westbound lane of US-50 was closed for a brief period of time at Maple Lake Road due to a mudslide.
State Route 78 near the town of McConnelsville was closed due to flooding of Four Mile Creek and Mans Fork.

Early in the afternoon on the 3rd, Sunday Creek in Glouster began to flood and spilled onto nearby fields and yards. A few hours later the heavy rain resulted in multiple road closures throughout the county. These included portions of State Route 690, State Route 550, State Route 56, and State Route 681.

Several roads in the county were closed due to flooding on the evening of February 3rd. These included State Route 145, State Route 821, and State Route 26. They would remain closed into the next day while high water issues were observed.

Several roads were closed across southern Gallia County by the evening of February 3rd due to flooding. These included portions State Route 218, State Route 141, and State Route 775. These roadways remained closed until the flood waters receded.
All eastbound lanes of State Route 554 were closed from Sisson Road to State Route 7 due to flooding. The roadway did not open until the floodwaters receded.

Large portions of roadways were closed from the evening of February 3rd until the 4th due to high water. These included State Route 349, State Route 160, and State Route 328 as well as Industrial Park Road near McArthur.
Portions of State Route 93 and State Route 775 were closed on the evening of February 3rd due to flooding. The roadways remained closed until the floodwaters receded.

Several major roadways were closed from the evening of February 3rd into the next day due to flooding. These included portions of State Route 143, State Route 681, and several portions State Route 124. The roads were able to open once again once the floodwaters receded.
Flooding occurred along several portions of Kentucky Route 5.
High water was observed along Old Lick Creek Road.
Flooding was observed near the 1900 Block along South State Highway 1.
High water flowed along Brush Creek Road near the 1600 Block.
High water flowed along Buffalo Branch Road.
Flooding occurred along Kentucky State Route 1 near the community of Fallsburg.
High water occurred over the intersection of Trace Road and Four Mile Road.
High water was observed over Walnut Street along US Route 23 in the city of Catlettsburg.
High water flowed over the intersection of Old Buckley Road and Kentucky Route 5.
High water occurred over the road near the intersection of Blackburn Avenue and Roberts Drive near the city of Ashland.
